2610.14169.abstract: Within the homogeneous framework for the derivation of GC ages defined by the CARMA collaboration, we focus on the clusters born in-situ in the MW. As they are the oldest among the old GCs, their absolute age provides constraints about the age of the Universe. Moreover, the shape of their AMR is expected to show the imprints of past merger events, in case these were able to trigger GC formation in the Galaxy. We derive new homogeneous ages for 18 GCs dynamically and/or chemically classified as in-situ, and build the MW AMR from a total sample of 34 GCs. We find that all the selected GCs follow a well defined AMR, with the exception of NGC6642 and Pal1. While the former is likely a member of the LKH merger event, thus putting chronological evidence for the existence of this progenitor on even more robust ground, for the latter we propose an alternative scenario according to which it formed in-situ, but in a metal-depleted region of the Galaxy, possibly due to the interaction with an unspecified merger event. To find evidence of merger-driven GC formation, we use a GMM for the observed age distribution. This is statistically best-fit by 4 components, which we associate with significant events of the MW merger history. Cluster ages were finally calibrated to a more accurate absolute age scale based on asteroseismic measurements of the mass of red giant stars in NGC6791, and the resulting AMR was fit to compute the look-back time for the beginning of cluster formation in the MW. The fit yields t_GC,i=13.59+0.33-0.32 Gyr for initial cluster formation, and tU=13.79+/-0.34 Gyr for the age of the Universe. This value translates to H0=68.72+3.95-3.49(stat.)+2.65-2.32(sys.) km s-1 Mpc-1, where the systematic error comes from a realistic estimate of the zero point uncertainty on the GC absolute ages derived from stellar models.

2610.14172.abstract: Understanding the reservoirs of iron (Fe) in our Galaxy is crucial for probing the mechanisms that drive dust grain growth in the interstellar medium (ISM). High-resolution X-ray absorption spectroscopy offers a powerful tool to investigate the chemistry of dust grains, particularly those containing Fe, through spectroscopic features near photoabsorption edges known as X-ray Absorption Fine Structures (XAFS). With the Resolve spectrometer aboard XRISM, we can now examine the Fe K-edge (7.1 keV) owing to its improved spectral resolution in this energy range. This enabled us to probe the dust grain chemistry in high Galactic column densities. In this work, we present a pilot study on dust grain chemistry through the Fe K-edge of the XRISM Performance Verification target GX 340+0. This source is a persistently bright low-mass X-ray binary with a hydrogen column density of 6.6x10^22 cm^-2 along the line of sight, providing sufficient optical depth at the Fe K-edge. By fitting combined dust and gas models, we find that Fe is depleted by 95% into dust along the line of sight towards the source. Moreover, we find evidence that 38% of the solid-phase Fe is in metallic iron, 47% in iron sulfides, and the remainder in silicates. The large contribution from metallic iron and iron sulfides differs from what is typically inferred from X-ray studies of diffuse ISM and may suggest that that these compounds become more significant reservoirs of Fe in higher column density Galactic sightlines.

2610.14174.abstract: We present a systematic interferometric search for close supermassive black hole (SMBH) binaries in 20 nearby type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGN) observed with VLTI/\grav. We investigate parsec-scale asymmetric emission by modeling the squared visibilities and closure phases with a single circular Gaussian component plus a background point source for the central AGN, and searching for additional compact companions through grid-based binary models. The robustness of the search is validated using injection-recovery simulations and point-spread-function diagnostics. Several features are identified in the initial significance maps, but only one candidate out of 20 shows a persistent compact asymmetry, corresponding to an observed incidence of $5\%$. If NGC~3783 is interpreted as a binary AGN, we derive a Poissonian one-sided $1\sigma$ upper limit of $f_{\rm bin}<16.5\%$ for GRAVITY-detectable binaries among bright nearby AGN (K<12.5) at separations of $\sim1$-$100$~pc. Conversely, if the observed asymmetry in NGC~3783 is associated with asymmetric circumnuclear dust emission, the corresponding upper limit on the binary fraction is $f_{\rm bin}<9.2\%$. We compare these results with predictions from the Horizon-AGN simulation, finding comparable binary fractions. We also noted that the expected fraction strongly depends on the assumed distribution of individual SMBH accretion rates within binaries, which is currently unresolved in cosmological models. Our results demonstrate the potential of infrared interferometry to identify parsec-scale binary AGN candidates and motivate future GRAVITY+ observations to expand the sample and follow up known candidates, helping to confirm their nature and distinguish genuine binaries from asymmetric nuclear structures.

2610.14179.abstract: We present direct $N$-body simulations of a stellar disc around the supermassive black hole Sgr~A*, perturbed by an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) and embedded in a live nuclear star cluster. A retrograde IMBH with $m_\bullet=2000\,M_\odot$, relative inclination $\theta_\bullet=150^\circ$, and initial semi-major axis $a_\bullet=0.15$~pc breaks the disc into three disc-like components and an angular momentum filament. The stochastic torques of the cluster, together with the IMBH's inward migration, increase the angular separation between these substructures. By ${\sim}5$~Myr, their separations become comparable to those among the observed Galactic-centre young star structures. The innermost ($a\le0.04$~pc) disc stars evolve into an S-star-like population. Relaxation driven by the cluster disperses their orbital planes, excites their eccentricities and depletes the `zone of avoidance' within ${\sim}10$~Myr even without an IMBH. The IMBH further accelerates their orbital-plane reorientation. However, the most eccentric S-stars may require an additional formation channel, such as the Hills mechanism. The distinctive signatures of the IMBH are the well-separated disc components and the eccentricity excitation confined to the radial range swept by its orbit. Dynamical friction from the cluster reduces the orbital size of a $2000\,M_\odot$ IMBH initially at $0.15$~pc by more than a factor of two within $10$~Myr. Prograde IMBHs tend to align with the stellar disc, whereas a $2000\,M_\odot$ retrograde IMBH can anti-align with the radially overlapping disc stars. We also quantify how the IMBH affects the supply of stars to the loss cone and the rates of stellar tidal disruptions and binary separations.

2610.14181.abstract: We introduce and describe the Globular cluster Observations for Luminosity-Dispersion distances (GOLD) project, which has the principal aim of determining independent distances based on the globular cluster (GC) absolute magnitude-velocity dispersion ($M_V - \sigma$) relation calibrated with Milky Way GCs with Gaia distances. The project comprises observations of GCs in 19 early- and late-type galaxies taken with FLAMES/GIRAFFE on ESO's Very Large Telescope. So far, 17 galaxies have been observed. The spectra cover the wavelength range 8483-9000 AA, including the calcium triplet region at a spectral resolution of $R\sim18,000$. The spectra provide line-of-sight velocities with typical uncertainties of $\Delta v = 1-2$ km s$^{-1}$. Using primarily velocities to separate extragalactic sources from foreground stars, we present here our initial sample of 1062 GCs and 101 ultra-compact dwarf galaxies (UCDs). For more than 650 of these objects we present the first velocity measurement. We discuss the available photometry and size measurements, and show that our velocities are in good agreement with previous studies. Our velocity catalogues are made publicly available. Beyond the principal aim of obtaining precision distances, additional science to be explored with these data includes host galaxy halo dynamics and clustering analysis, mass-to light ratios of GCs and UCDs in the sample, the stellar initial mass function and black hole occupation fraction of the GCs, and chemical abundances from high-dispersion spectra.

2610.14618.abstract: The flux variability of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) is commonly modeled using the damped random walk (DRW), but increasingly rich multiband time-domain surveys motivate more flexible stochastic models that characterize variability beyond a single timescale and exploit dependence across bands. Multivariate continuous-time autoregressive moving average (MCARMA) processes extend the multivariate DRW to higher-order stochastic dynamics and provide a matrix-valued power spectral density for characterizing marginal variability and cross-band dependence. In a carefully selected Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Stripe~82 sample, higher-order models are selected for 109 of 134 AGNs (81.3\%), with substantial rather than marginal support in most objects; convergence diagnostics indicate that this fraction is conservative. The fitted models also reveal strong cross-band dependence that generally decreases with wavelength separation. Motivated by this richer structure, we investigate its recoverability under Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) observing conditions. Model-order recovery depends strongly on the underlying stochastic behavior as well as source brightness and observing cadence. Recovery is high across many of the simulated settings, but deteriorates when the characteristic features of higher-order variability become difficult to distinguish from the multivariate DRW. Additional simulations show that this loss of distinguishability can persist over a range of underlying variability behaviors. These results show that stochastic structure beyond the multivariate DRW is prevalent in our selected SDSS sample, while its recoverability with LSST depends on both observational conditions and the form of the underlying stochastic variability. The methodology is implemented in the Python package mcarma.

2610.14653.abstract: We present resolved optical integral-field spectroscopy of the 32 luminous and ultraluminous infrared galaxy systems of the Multiphase Analysis of (U)LIRG Nuclear Activity (MAUNA) sample, drawn from the GOALS survey and selected to have JWST/MIRI medium-resolution spectrometer (MRS) observations. The data set combines new Keck/KCWI observations of 10 systems with archival VLT/MUSE cubes for 22 systems, covering H$\beta$ to [S II] at ~1 arcsecond spatial resolution (~0.9 kpc at the sample median distance). Using the optical [N II]/H$\alpha$ BPT diagram, we find that composite and LINER-like excitation together account for most of the classified area (median fractions 0.44 and 0.26), while Seyfert-like gas covers a median fraction of 0.02 but carries a far larger proportion of the line luminosity where it is present. Both the projected size of the Seyfert-classified region, $R_{\rm Sy}=0.08$-$7.5$ kpc, and its [O III] luminosity increase with the bolometric AGN luminosity, with $R_{\rm Sy}\propto L_{\rm AGN,bol}^{0.54\pm0.18}$, as expected for gas photoionized at a constant ionization parameter. The scatter about the luminosity relation depends on dust opacity: the [O III] luminosity per unit AGN luminosity falls by $1.09\pm0.25$ dex per unit depth of the 9.7 $\mu$m silicate absorption feature (Spearman $\rho=-0.60$, $p=0.001$). Optical excitation diagnostics therefore locate AGN-excited gas reliably but systematically underestimate the luminosity the AGN supplies to the host in the most obscured (U)LIRGs.

2610.15007.abstract: The spatial structures of chemical populations constrain Galactic disk evolution and its underlying physical processes. Gaia XP spectra provide one of the largest spectroscopic samples available. We use Gaia XP spectra to study Galactic disk mono-abundance populations (MAPs), measuring their scale heights as a function of radius and radial surface-mass-density profiles. We construct a red giant branch (RGB) sample and divide it into MAPs according to $[\alpha/{\rm M}]$ and $[{\rm M/H}]$. The sample covers a $6\times6$ kpc region centered on the Sun in the Galactic plane and extends to $|Z|<3.7$ kpc. We estimate XP completeness using a Gaia photometric parent sample and combine PARSEC isochrones with a Kroupa initial mass function (IMF) to calculate the selection function and convert observed stellar counts into intrinsic stellar mass densities. We fit vertical density profiles with an exponential model to derive scale heights and integrate the fitted profiles to obtain surface mass densities. The resulting profiles are generally consistent with those from APOGEE. All MAPs show flaring, with the high-$\alpha$ population exhibiting the strongest flaring and the metal-poor and sub-solar low-$\alpha$ populations showing the weakest. Surface-mass-density profiles differ significantly among MAPs: the high-$\alpha$ and metal-rich low-$\alpha$ populations show approximately exponential declines, whereas the other low-$\alpha$ populations exhibit plateau-like features, indicating that the Galactic disk cannot be described by a simple single-exponential profile. These differential structures suggest a complex Galactic disk assembly history likely regulated by birth conditions, secular dynamical heating, radial migration, and external perturbations.

2610.15031.abstract: Blue horizontal-branch (BHB) stars are ideal tracers for mapping the structure of the Galactic stellar halo. However, traditional spectroscopic identification is limited by data quality and sample size, while broad-band photometric methods often achieve only moderate completeness and purity. Building upon the color-space BHB identification method of \citet{2025ApJS..278...62H}, we synthesize SkyMapper $(u,v,g,z)$ photometry from DESI MWS DR1 spectroscopy and identify 9,237 BHB candidates in the $(g-z)_0$--$(u-v)_0$ color space using the HDBSCAN clustering algorithm. We then construct a Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) Bayesian probability model with capture-recapture (C-R) prior to assign posterior membership probabilities, achieving a probability-weighted purity of 88.9\% and completeness of 94.2\%. Applying an escape-velocity cut based on the Galactic gravitational potential, we remove 1,461 contaminants with unphysical kinematic parameters, yielding a clean photometric BHB sample $\mathcal{S}_c$ of 7,776 stars (retention rate $R_{\rm keep} = 84.2\%$). Systematic analysis of the contaminants reveals that they are predominantly faint sources ($g\sim20$~mag) with very low signal-to-noise ratios (median SNR~$<$~5). When the BHB color--luminosity relation is incorrectly applied to these objects, their space velocities are amplified beyond the Galactic escape limit, confirming that the escape-velocity filter essentially acts as a physical detector of low-SNR--driven distance inflation.

2610.15071.abstract: Dwarf galaxies exhibit a large diversity in rotation curve shapes, challenging galaxy formation models within the $\Lambda$CDM paradigm. We present NIVARIA-LG, a new suite of cosmological simulations studying dwarf galaxy evolution in realistic Local Group environments. This intermediate-resolution pilot lays the groundwork for the full-scale NIVARIA project. The simulations combine constrained Local Group initial conditions from HESTIA with the NIHAO galaxy formation model. The simulated galaxies reproduce observed stellar-to-halo mass relations, match the Baryonic Tully-Fisher relation, and capture the distribution of stellar effective radii, including compact and diffuse galaxies. We analyse the structural and kinematic properties of isolated dwarf galaxies with $10^7 \lesssim M_\star/M_\odot \lesssim 10^{10}$, focusing on rotation curve diversity. NIVARIA-LG naturally produces a broad range of rotation curve shapes, including slowly rising systems underrepresented in previous simulations and steep rotation curves. We find that rotation curve diversity is primarily associated with gas extent and inner dark matter structure: more extended gas and shallower inner density profiles correspond to more slowly rising curves, while stellar effective radius shows little independent association. Individual galaxies show that rotation curve shapes change rapidly as gas is redistributed during assembly. Recent accretion events are also associated with more slowly rising curves in the most massive dwarfs. Together, these results suggest that rotation curve diversity is linked to the baryonic cycle, which shapes the inner dark matter distribution. The Local Group environment and its filaments influence this evolution by regulating gas accretion and redistribution, producing the observed diversity in rotation curve shapes.

2610.15255.abstract: Anisotropic ionizing radiation is a natural theoretical expectation for super-Eddington accretion in active galactic nuclei (AGNs), implying that the ionizing flux incident on the broad-line region (BLR) clouds differs from that measured along the observer's line of sight. Reverberation mapping studies have revealed systematically shortened time lags of the broad H$\beta$ emission line relative to continuum variations in super-Eddington AGNs, a phenomenon that can be naturally interpreted as a consequence of anisotropic ionizing continuum radiation. To further investigate this anisotropy, we perform a systematic analysis of the H$\beta$ line responsivity, defined as the ratio of the variability amplitude of H$\beta$ to that of the driving continuum, for both sub- and super-Eddington AGNs. By combining the effective responsivities measured relative to the driving continuum, after correcting for the continuum--emission-line delay, with photoionization calculations, we infer the ionizing radiation field received by their BLRs. We find that, in super-Eddington AGNs, the ionizing flux inferred from the H$\beta$ responsivity differs significantly from that observed along the line of sight, whereas the two are in closer agreement in sub-Eddington AGNs. These results provide compelling evidence for strong anisotropy of the incident ionizing radiation in super-Eddington AGNs. We conclude by discussing the broader implications of this anisotropy, including its potential relevance to the "little red dots" recently discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope.

2610.15295.abstract: This study investigates the chemical evolution history and radial migration in the Milky Way utilizing high-precision age measurements based on large-scale stellar spectroscopic surveys. Recent observational data have revealed a distinct break in the age-metallicity relation of stars in the solar neighborhood, suggesting that stellar populations of the Milky Way can be divided into two evolutionary sequences. Based on galactic chemical evolution models, we confirm that this break in the age-metallicity relation can be explained by a recent major gas accretion event, which diluted the metallicity in the disk and triggered a starburst, leading to the formation of an independent age-metallicity sequence. To assess the impact of stellar radial migration, we incorporate a simplified treatment of this process into our multi-zone chemical evolution model. Radial migration is modeled as a probabilistic diffusion process, characterized by a Gaussian distribution. By fitting the model-predicted metallicity distribution functions (MDFs) of mono-age stellar populations to observations, we infer a migration strength of $\sigma = 2.15^{+0.100}_{-0.103}\,{\rm kpc}$ for stars with ages between 2 and 6 Gyr located at 9.5-11.5 kpc, corresponding to an average radial displacement of 1.92 kpc over 10 Gyr. This result is lower than previous estimates of stellar radial migration, suggesting that the role of radial migration in shaping the chemical structure of the Milky Way is less important than previously estimated.

2610.15349.abstract: We investigate the metallicity dependence of the tilt of the velocity ellipsoid using more than 572,000 stars selected from GALAH and Gaia. We find that the tilt angles of disk stars can be well described by the relation $\alpha = \alpha_{0}\,\mathrm{arctan}(Z/R)$, and the $\alpha_{0}$ differ significantly among different disk populations, with $\alpha_{0}$ are 0.78 $\pm$ 0.05, 0.86 $\pm$ 0.07, and 0.77 $\pm$ 0.07 for the whole sample, the Low-[$\alpha$/Fe] and the High-[$\alpha$/Fe] populations, respectively. These results indicate that Galactic disk populations are globally tilted toward cylindrical alignment, implying that the gravitational potential of the Galactic baryonic disk plays a dominant role in shaping the kinematics of dynamically relaxed stars. Our detailed analysis further reveals a metallicity dependence of $\alpha_{0}$ for various populations, with the Low-[$\alpha$/Fe] and the High-[$\alpha$/Fe] populations are respectively $\alpha_{0}$ = 0.12 $\mathrm{sin}$(3.72 [Fe/H] + 1.09) + 0.75 and $\alpha_{0}$ = 0.20 $\mathrm{sin}$(2.99 [Fe/H] + 1.90) + 0.71. These results indicate that the metallicity dependence observed in the Low-[$\alpha$/Fe] population may be primarily associated with resonances induced by the Galactic bar, while the behavior of the High-[$\alpha$/Fe] population may also have been affected by additional dynamical and evolutionary processes, such as violent heating associated with mergers, accretion, and/or the formation of these stars in an environment shaped by mergers of gas-rich systems and/or a turbulent ISM.

2610.15901.abstract: Charting the evolution of star-formation, stellar mass and dust build-up over cosmic time relies on the accurate characterisation of the stellar population properties of high redshift galaxies. We present a catalogue of spectroscopically derived physical properties for ~12,000 galaxies at z>2, with archival JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectroscopy and JWST/NIRCam imaging from the DAWN JWST Archive. We present a custom version of the SED fitting code BAGPIPES, used to perform joint spectrophotometric modelling of PRISM spectra and broadband NIRCam photometry. In doing so, we publicly release a science-ready catalogue of the physical properties of galaxies beyond cosmic noon. We report key physical properties, such as stellar masses, star-formation rates (SFR) and timescales, and V-band dust attenuation (Av). We further probe the recent star-formation histories (SFH) of galaxies via their SFRs on 3 Myr, 10 Myr, and 100 Myr timescales, capturing both rising and falling recent SFHs. Through dust-corrected ugi colour-colour diagrams of massive galaxies, we show how quiescent and dusty galaxies populate this colour space at z>2, with galaxies experiencing a recent downturn in star-formation occupying distinct parameter space. We also study the dustiest galaxies in our sample, showing that they are preferentially more massive and strongly star-forming relative to the parent sample, residing on the high-mass end of the star-forming main-sequence. The slope of the attenuation curve has a strong dependence on Av, varying from steep to shallow as the dust attenuation increases and the specific star-formation rate decreases. Our findings show that the unparalleled number statistics of this catalogue of spectroscopically derived stellar population properties uniquely enables the study star-formation, quenching and dust properties of galaxies from cosmic noon to cosmic dawn.

2610.15946.abstract: The ancient stellar populations and simple structure of the local dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs) make them excellent laboratories for studying the chemical evolution of the early universe. In this paper, we fit one-zone galactic chemical evolution models to C, Mg, Si, Ca, Fe, Sr, Y, Ba, and Eu abundances in the dSphs Sculptor and Draco. By including the s- and r-processes in our model, we are able to place constraints on the timescale of r-process enrichment in these dSphs. We find that neutron star mergers cannot be the only source of the r-process in Sculptor and Draco, and that a prompt r-process source is required to explain the observed stellar abundances. When neutron star mergers are the only source of the r-process in our models, their minimum delay time must be just 14-16 Myr. The neutron-capture abundances in Sculptor and Draco can also be fit by models with a longer neutron star merger minimum delay time combined with a prompt r-process source that operates on the same timescale as massive star evolution, such as magneto-rotational supernovae. Additionally, the Sr and Y abundances in the dSphs set limits on the Sr and Y yields per r-process event. We find that theoretical r-process yields overestimate Sr and Y production by a factor of up to 100.

2610.16007.abstract: We present TractorJAX, an open-source GPU reimplementation of the catalog-forced mode of The Tractor. We use it to test whether regularization or external flux priors enable reliable fitting of reference catalogs that extend below the depth directly constrained by undersampled SPHEREx images. For full-depth regularized fits, TractorJAX fits $100\times100$-pixel cutouts at 11.9 ms each on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. In simulated images of the Abell 2537 galaxy-cluster field, extending the fitted catalog from $m_z<21$ to the full DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys DR10 catalog increases the scatter in fractional flux residuals by 34%, even with regularization. We also test the methods using SPHEREx observations in nine fields, assessing the number of reliably measured sources and photometric-redshift accuracy. Requiring S/N $>5$ in more than half of the 102 channels, we find that the regularized full-depth fit yields 40% fewer sources than the truncated fit. For sources meeting this requirement in both fits, the normalized median absolute deviation of the photometric redshifts, $\sigma_{\rm NMAD}$, is 17% larger in the full-depth fit. External flux priors recover nearly as many sources as the $m_z<21$ fit, but increase $\sigma_{\rm NMAD}$ by 0.0015 for the common calibrated sample. Neither regularization nor the external flux priors tested here simultaneously preserve the sample size and photometric-redshift accuracy achieved by the truncated fit. Our results suggest that the optimal fitted-catalog depth cannot be determined from image-level performance alone, but should be selected through end-to-end tests tailored to the intended science measurement.

2610.16057.abstract: Current-generation 21-cm surveys of extragalactic neutral hydrogen (HI) with instruments such as FAST and ASKAP are providing detailed spectral and spatial information for over 10^5 galaxies. Future HI surveys with next-generation radio telescopes could provide sample sizes larger by orders of magnitude. There is therefore a need for accurate, automated, and reliable parameterisation of the HI emission from galaxies. We have developed an automated estimator for HI global profile widths to better enable studies of, for example, dynamical masses and Tully-Fisher distances. Our estimator is based on an implementation of the BusyFit profile-fitting algorithm, and converges for 95% of global profiles in the WALLABY pilot survey. Probability density functions are calculated for all profile parameters using Monte Carlo techniques, and example error parameterisations are given. We confirm that linewidth uncertainties depend primarily on the integrated signal-to-noise ratio, profile steepness, and the linewidth, consistent with previous studies. We compare several common linewidth definitions, and the width at 50% of the mean flux density (Wm50) is found to be the most robust measure of linewidth. We provide examples of the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation drawn from the WALLABY pilot survey.

2610.16200.abstract: We study the intrinsic 0.5--2~keV emission of the hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) in the IllustrisTNG simulation TNG100-2 at redshifts 0, 0.1, and 0.2. We calculate the emission of gas cells with $T \geq 10^6$~K in the spherical shell between $0.15R_{500}$ and $R_{500}$ and compare samples selected by their star-formation activity. X-ray luminosity increases with halo mass, although the class-dependent fits cover different mass intervals. Among galaxies with positive luminosity and star formation rate (SFR), the high-activity sample retains a positive association after a linear adjustment for halo mass. The residual association is weaker in the quiescent subset with positive luminosity and SFR. Within $10^{11.75}<M_{500}/M_\odot<10^{12.25}$, the high-activity sample has more centrally concentrated emission and a median luminosity about five times that of the quiescent sample. The two populations have similar median hot-gas masses despite their different X-ray luminosities and radial profiles. These differences are consistent with variations in the spatial distribution and thermodynamic state of the emitting gas, although the samples are not matched in halo mass. Our results suggest that soft X-ray emission probes the structure of the hot CGM as well as its gas content, offering a way to investigate how star formation and feedback shape gaseous halos.

2610.16265.abstract: Using DESI photometric catalog data, we systematically analyze the spatial alignment of star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and quiescent galaxies (QGs) in clusters. The results reveal that, in both brightest central galaxy (BCG) alignment (BA) and satellite alignment (SA), the alignment signals of SFGs and QGs exhibit opposite trends in several aspects. For the BA signal, SFGs show stronger alignment in cluster outskirts, whereas QGs exhibit stronger alignment in inner regions. For the SA signal, both SFGs and QGs exhibit nearly isotropic signals in outer regions, while in inner regions they show opposite signals. In addition, the BA signal depends on cluster richness and QG fraction, and is more pronounced in mature clusters. Specifically, QGs show a stronger BA signal overall, which increases with luminosity and axis ratio, whereas SFGs show a weaker BA signal with no significant dependence on these parameters. The BA signal also exhibits a strong dependence on satellite galaxy color, which is independent of morphology. We confirm this by analyzing the BA signal in two populations: red disk and blue elliptical galaxies. However, neither BA nor SA shows a significant dependence on redshift at z < 0.5. In summary, these findings reflect how galaxy transport along cosmic filaments drives cluster evolution: early-stage SFGs fall into clusters along filaments, and during cluster relaxation, their spatial orientations are reshaped by gravitational potentials and tidal forces, weakening BA signal and enhancing SA signal. In contrast, QGs, as early cluster members, exhibit a more pronounced anisotropic distribution and maintain relatively stable spatial orientations.

Panel (b): detected metal absorption lines and corresponding best-fit metal abundances relative to solar: the carbon, oxygen and silicon abundances are the lowest ever observed by factors $3-4$. The carbon abundance being less than $-$4 establishes the object as the first “ultra” metal-poor DLA.

Figure 2: Redshift evolution of the $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$-element abundance of DLAs. UMP–DLA–1 (black point inside the large red star) displays an abundance of $\alpha$ element to hydrogen 5000 times below solar and over three times lower than any other DLA (black points). Its redshift of 5.14 suggests the presence of a metallicity floor which increases with cosmic time. The dashed gray line indicates the previously known most metal-poor DLA, [$\alpha$/H]$=-$3.22.

Figure 3: The transition discriminant. With sufficiently low abundances of oxygen and carbon, UMP–DLA–1 (red star) is the first gas reservoir detected below the transition discriminant[2] (grey area, with uncertainties in light grey) where the IMF is known to be top-heavy. It follows the trend seen in extremely metal-poor and very metal-poor DLAs (black points) of a slight carbon deficit compared to oxygen, while individual metal-poor local stars (blue points, from SAGA[25]) display far more scatter. Characteristic uncertainties for stellar abundances are shown in the bottom-right corner. The purple circle represents the lowest-metallicity galaxy discovered in emission to date[10].

Figure 4: Enrichment pattern. UMP–DLA–1 (red) shows a deficit of carbon compared to $\alpha$ elements (O, Si) which is very similar to that observed in the second-most metal-poor DLA (orange) and in extremely metal-poor (EMP) DLAs. Vertical bars show the full range of measurements within each sample. The same chemical signature is seen in some EMP stars in ultra-faint dwarf galaxies; Boötes-1137 is shown as an example (purple, with vertical bars showing measurement uncertainties). Meanwhile, DLAs which are only very metal-poor do not share the observed carbon-to-oxygen deficit (blue).

2610.16509.abstract: Excitation of carbon and oxygen ions is the primary mechanism by which collapsing gas clouds dissipate heat to form new stars. At early cosmic times, in galaxies with chemically pristine gas, many stars are expected to have masses far larger than the mass of our sun due to the deficit in these elements. We searched for ultra-metal-poor galaxies using their spectroscopic absorption signatures in front of bright background quasars, employing the new GHOST high-resolution spectrograph. Here we report the discovery of the first galaxy containing a reservoir of neutral hydrogen gas with metallicity below the ultra-metal-poor threshold: with a measured carbon-to-hydrogen ratio 11,000 times lower than the Sun, it is the most pristine ever found by a factor of four. UMP-DLA-1 is the only known galaxy with measured carbon and oxygen abundances too low to enable efficient formation of stars with solar mass or below. The low metallicity alone therefore guarantees a top-heavy stellar population, providing a direct view of the chemical composition imprinted by massive low-metallicity stars that perished long before the present day: an elevated oxygen-to-carbon ratio. The abundance pattern of UMP-DLA-1 is likely a close representation of the atomic yields of first- or early second-generation stars.

2610.16710.abstract: We examine whether the unusual spatial flattening and orbital-plane coherence of the Milky Way's classical satellites are connected to the Galaxy's location in the cosmic web. We compare the 11 classical satellites with the 11 most massive satellites of 11,922 Milky Way-mass hosts in the TNG300-1 hydrodynamical simulation. We measure flattening with both the simple inertia tensor (SIT), which retains radial information, and the reduced inertia tensor (RIT), which isolates angular anisotropy. Orbital-plane coherence is characterized by the minimum opening angle containing the axes of the eight most coplanar satellite orbits. For the Milky Way, we find $(c/a,b/a)=(0.183,0.558)$ for SIT and $(0.364,0.736)$ for RIT, together with an eight-orbit opening angle of $21.9^\circ$. The corresponding fractions of simulated systems at least as extreme are $4.94\%$, $12.28\%$, and $5.04\%$, respectively. We describe the environment using the velocity-shear tensor smoothed on $2\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ and compare the full sample with Local Group-like pairs, systems whose shear eigenvalues match those reconstructed for the Local Group, and hosts in knots, filaments, sheets, and voids. Among the well-sampled environmental subsets, the shape and opening-angle distributions differ only weakly. Although the cosmic web imprints preferred orientations on host spins and satellite orbital-plane axes, the Milky Way combines orientations that are uncommon in the simulation. We conclude that the present-day cosmic-web environment alone does not substantially increase the occurrence of Milky Way-like satellite configurations. This result does not rule out an origin in anisotropic accretion, since neither the present-day web class nor its shear eigenvalues fully encodes the assembly history of an individual satellite system.

2610.16805.title: Evidence for Hierarchical Turbulent Scaling in Nearby Star-Forming Galaxies

figures.caption: Figure 1: Our analysis of each galaxy, illustrated for NGC 3621. Panel (a) shows the line of sight intensity-weighted mean velocity, the “moment 1” map from the PHANGS-ALMA dataset. Panel (b) shows the residual map after subtraction of the rotational model $V_{model}$, which removes large scale galaxy kinematics. Panel (c) shows the structure functions $S_{p}(\ell)^{1/p}$ in $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ for $p=1$ to $6$. The shaded area marks the fitted range, from twice the beam FWHM to the scale where power law behavior breaks down. Panel (d) shows the extended self-similarity (ESS) exponents $\beta_{p}$, computed by fitting $\log S_{p}$ against $\log S_{3}$. Panel (e) shows the $\beta$ test from Padoan et al. [34], whose slope gives the cascade ratio $\beta_{\mathrm{SL}}$. We repeat the steps in panels (c) to (e) in each of $N=1000$ bootstrap iterations to estimate $\zeta_{p}$, $\beta_{p}$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{SL}}$ with their uncertainties as the 16th and 84th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution.

For the blue line, we fix the slope at $p/(p+1)$ and fit only the intercept in $\zeta_{p}=\frac{p}{p+1}\zeta_{p+1}+\gamma$. For comparison, the red line evaluates the model at the population medians of $\beta_{SL}$ and $\alpha$.

Each label is the Mach number of the assigned simulation. A range is shown when two simulation curves bracket the observed exponents.

Figure S3: Linear interdependence of consecutive scaling exponents of the 52 PHANGS-ALMA galaxies that yield power law scaling. The panels show $\zeta_{p}$ versus $\zeta_{p+1}$ for each galaxy, with error bars from the bootstrap procedure. The black line shows our fit of $\zeta_{p}=m\cdot\zeta_{p+1}+b$, with slope and intercept free. The blue line fixes the slope at $p/(p+1)$ and fits only the intercept in $\zeta_{p}=\frac{p}{p+1}\zeta_{p+1}+\gamma$. The red line evaluates the model at the medians of $\beta_{SL}$ and $\alpha$ from the 31 selected galaxies.

Figure S4: The first to third order scaling exponents $\zeta_{p}$ for 100 molecular clouds computed by Ma et al. [29] plotted against their consecutive exponent $\zeta_{p+1}$. An ordinary linear least-squares fit provides slopes of 0.519 and 0.646, which are close to the $p/(p+1)$ reference coefficients.

2610.16805.abstract: We find recurring signatures of intermittency in molecular-gas velocities from cloud to galactic scales. In 31 selected galaxies from PHANGS-ALMA, velocity-centroid exponents through sixth order show nonlinear order dependence and nearly linear relations between consecutive exponents across galaxies. Positive estimated offsets from single-exponent scaling occur in all 52 galaxies with a valid power law fit and 99 of 100 clouds. A generalized She-Leveque hierarchy accommodates these signatures, supporting a hierarchical description of turbulent scaling in molecular gas across these environments.

2610.16936.abstract: Diffuse X-ray emission in galaxies originates from stellar-feedback-heated gas and unresolved compact sources. We investigate its thermal component and the scaling of X-ray luminosity with star formation rate (SFR), including galaxies with very low SFRs. We analyzed eROSITA/SRG data from the four all-sky surveys (eRASS:4) for a blind, volume-limited sample of 140 galaxies within 25 Mpc from the Updated Nearby Galaxy Catalog (Karachentsev et al. 2013), cross-matched with HECATEv2 (Kyritsis et al. 2026b). Early-type galaxies were analyzed separately, while star-forming galaxies were divided into low-, medium-, and high-specific-SFR (sSFR) subsamples. We modeled the integrated X-ray spectra with thermal plasma and power-law components, stacked spectra for each subsample, and derived total and thermal X-ray luminosities. The stacked spectra show a stronger soft thermal component at high sSFR, whereas low-sSFR and early-type galaxies are increasingly dominated by the harder non-thermal continuum. For star-forming galaxies, the total 0.5-8 keV luminosity follows $\log L_X \sim 39.5 + 0.9\log\mathrm{SFR}$, with an intrinsic scatter of about 0.9 dex. The 0.5-2 keV thermal luminosity follows $\log L_X \sim 38.7 + 1.1\log\mathrm{SFR}$, with an intrinsic scatter of about 0.7 dex. The thermal luminosity remains well correlated with SFR down to $\sim 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ and is consistent with previous relations for star-forming galaxies. By contrast, the flatter and more scattered total X-ray luminosity-SFR relation suggests that unresolved X-ray binaries likely dominate at low SFR, while thermal X-ray emission remains a robust tracer of stellar feedback.

2610.16982.abstract: We use Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) light curves to identify photometrically selected changing-state active galactic nucleus (CSAGN) candidates. We employ unsupervised deep learning and anomaly detection methods to identify unusual patterns of variability in the light curves of 872,228 AGNs with known variability. We find that 8,504 light curves show anomalous behavior. Among these, 682 sources show evidence for two-state photometric behavior during the Gaia DR3 observing baseline. These 682 CSAGN candidates were selected using an automated statistical pattern recognition approach based on Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to identify sources whose magnitude distributions are consistent with two preferred brightness levels, substantially reducing the need for human visual inspection in selecting the CSAGN candidates. The candidates tend to have fainter absolute magnitudes and lower redshifts than the non-anomalous Gaia variable AGN sample, suggesting that some may be accreting at lower rates. Our approach builds a large candidate sample with less reliance on human visual selection. Follow-up observations of these sources can help identify what drives changing-state transitions and clarify their connection to accretion-disk physics and supermassive black hole (SMBH) fueling.

2610.17051.abstract: Favored carriers of the Diffuse Interstellar Bands (DIBs) are carbonaceous molecules whose constituents have been presumably expelled by dying stars along with those of dust grains. The parallel evolution of DIB carriers and grains and their potential interplay are unknown. We assembled published R(V) measurements of 505 hot stars. We inverted a catalog of extinction data based on Gaia XP spectra and NIR photometry, and used the resulting new 3D extinction map to locate the opaque areas responsible for R(V) for each star. Using archived spectra, we measured their 5780, 5797 and 8620 A DIBs. In parallel, we compared local and line-of-sight (LOS) R(V)s from recent 3D maps with local and LOS Gaia DIB strengths from our recent map. Results: R(V)s from hot stars reveal variations on large spatial scales, confirming with independent data the published 3D pattern. Gaia DIB strength maps show large spatial scale variations similar to those of R(V) maps, with higher abundance of DIB carriers corresponding to higher R(V). LOS Gaia DIB strengths and R(V)s from 3D maps also correlate positively in the R(V) range 2.3-3.4, but there is no connection for higher R(V), likely due to the disappearance of DIB carriers in dense clouds. Despite averaging effects along the LOS to hot stars, we find differences in R(V)-DIB relationships among the three DIBs, with an evolution from negative to positive correlation from the zeta- to the sigma-type DIBs. This can be understood in the frame of the bimodal evolution of R(V) with the extinction, with the zeta (resp. sigma) DIB carrier disappearance in the decreasing (resp. increasing) phase of R(V). Various combinations of DIB strengths and DIB ratios may allow to define the range of R(V), but the relationship between DIBs and R(V) also appears to depend on the wavelength range used to determine R(V).

2610.17216.title: Magnetic field evolution in feedback-dominated galaxies

Figure 9: Mass-weighted $B-n_{\rm H}$ and $f_{\rm B}-n_{\rm H}$ (see the main text for definition of $f_{\rm B}$) distribution histograms for gas with $r\leq 150\,{\rm kpc}$. Similar to what we saw in Section 5.1, going from FIRE-2 to FIRE-3, the B-field strength increases slightly, while the magnetic-to-turbulent ratio $f_{\rm B}$ bumps up much more.

2610.17216.abstract: Over the last decade, magnetic fields (B-fields) have become a common ingredient in galaxy formation simulations. Although seemingly unimportant in matching observational constraints such as the $M_*-M_{\rm halo}$ relations, the B-field influences the circumgalactic medium (CGM) gas and determines cosmic ray (CR) propagation, making it an indispensable non-thermal component. Nevertheless, the intricate physics of B-fields, particularly how they evolve to the observed $\mu$G-level field, remains largely elusive. In this work, we systematically address the evolution of B-fields over cosmic time using the FIRE-2 (Feedback In Realistic Environments) magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations. We present results for both Milky Way (MW)-mass and dwarf galaxies, with and without CRs. We find that CRs have little impact on B-field properties, while the halo mass controls the saturated B-field strength at $z\sim 0$. However, all runs reach a halo-independent magnetic-to-turbulent ratio of $f_{\rm B}\sim 1-10\%$, though the methods used to measure turbulence could affect this value. We identify a three-stage evolutionary course for the B-field in tandem with galaxy formation: i. expansion, ii. amplification, and iii. saturation. The feature is universal, though the timings depend on the initial location and star formation history of the gas. Flux-freezing is the predominant driver for the first and last stages, exhibiting power relations $B\sim \rho^{2/3}$ and $\rho^{1/2}$, although the latter could also be explained by dynamical and energetic equilibria. The intermediate amplification stage, potentially driven by ``dynamos'', is fuelled by structure formation, feedback, and gas turbulence. We conjecture a numerically triggered, turbulence-driven amplification process to explain this phenomenon.

2610.17255.abstract:
We studied librating orbits of stars near the Outer Lindblad Resonance (OLR) of the bar using the angle-action variables of Hamiltonian dynamics. The librating orbits change the direction of their elongation relative to the major axis of the bar in a limited range of angles. To calculate orbits, we used the model of the Galaxy with an analytical bar which reproduces well the distributions of the observed stellar velocities along the Galactocentric distance R derived from the Gaia DR3 data. We compared the values of the orbital oscillation period of a typical star obtained from the theory and with the use of numerical simulation. Both values were found to be in good agreement and are equal to 2.0 Gyr. It was shown that the change in the average orbital radius, , of a star, calculated over the time interval of one radial oscillation, is regulated by the change in the direction of orbital elongation. As the orbit is tilted relative to the minor axis of the bar in the sense of Galactic rotation, the angular momentum of the star, L, decreases, on average, causing a decrease in . As the orbit is tilted in the opposite direction, and increase. We derived a general formula for the oscillation frequency, omega, of orbits captured by libration near the OLR of the bar. It turned out that the ratio of the frequency of orbit oscillations to the epicyclic frequency, omega/kappa, is determined by the parameters q_R and

, where the factor q_R is the ratio of the amplitude of the radial force generated by the bar to the average radial force produced by the entire galaxy at the distance of the OLR, and the parameter

characterizes the average elongation of orbits captured by libration near the OLR.

2610.17342.abstract: Intermittency is a fundamental property of astrophysical turbulence because it concentrates strong gradients, dissipation, and transport into rare, localized structures. In the multiphase interstellar medium (ISM), turbulent driving is especially important because the balance between compressive and solenoidal motions can regulate how extreme fluctuations are distributed among thermal phases. Yet conventional increment statistics quantify intermittency without identifying the structures that host it. We analyze three matched ideal-MHD simulations of a thermally multiphase neutral medium that differ only in the compressive fraction of the driving. Density, velocity, and magnetic-field increments are non-Gaussian in every thermal phase. Increasing compressive driving redistributes density and magnetic fluctuations preferentially into the cold gas rather than uniformly enhancing them across phases. We identify the structures associated with extreme increments using local, scale-matched diagnostics of compression, thermal gradients, vorticity, strain, magnetic curl, and magnetic tension. Extreme magnetic increments preferentially occur where magnetic curl and magnetic tension are simultaneously enhanced, more strongly than extreme velocity increments are associated with their kinematic hosts. Extreme velocity increments show comparable enrichment in vorticity and strain, whereas extreme density increments preferentially trace converging flows and thermal gradients only in the unstable medium. These associations weaken beyond a phase-dependent coherence scale. Our results show that turbulent driving controls how intermittency is partitioned among thermal phases, while distinct physical structures host extreme density, velocity, and magnetic fluctuations.

2610.17359.title: Untangling Similarities and Differences in Star Formation Histories Across Cosmological Simulations

figures.caption: Figure 1: The $z=0$ star-forming main sequence (SFMS) for each of the seven simulations in our sample (EAGLE: green, Illustris: light blue, IllustrisTNG: dark blue, Mufasa: orange, Simba: yellow, SC-SAM: pink, UniverseMachine: violet), with the combined distribution shown in the large bottom-right panel. Coloured points lie above each simulation’s mass cut ($M_{\star}>10^{9}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$, marked with solid red; $M_{\star}>10^{10}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ for Mufasa and Simba, marked with dashed red) and are included in our final sample; grey points lie below the cut and are excluded. The per-simulation colour scheme shown here is reused throughout this work; see Section II.2 for details on the cuts, per-simulation sample sizes, and visualization conventions. The seven simulations produce roughly consistent galaxy populations at $z=0$ on the scaling observables against which they were calibrated – though features such as the secondary-sequence structure visible in UniverseMachine already hint at implementation-level differences. This makes it unclear if the evolutionary pathways leading to these consistent present-day populations are themselves consistent, or whether distinct histories are hidden behind their matching $z=0$ properties.

Figure 2: Sample specific star formation histories (sSFHs) drawn from each simulation, after the data preparation described in Section II.2, in 1 dex stellar mass bins $\in[10^{9},10^{12}]\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ increasing from left to right; the leftmost bins for Mufasa and Simba are left blank by construction. From these samples it is already clear that similar sSFHs profiles can be produced across all simulations, while some simulations are able to produce more distinct profiles, such as the burstiness on short time scales exhibited by Mufasa, Simba, and EAGLE [56]. The mass binning also demonstrates why grouping by similar $M_{\star}$ alone is not sufficient to adequately compare sSFH profiles – as especially evident in the middle panels for Universe Machine and IllustrisTNG, showing sSFHs with substantially different growth rates, peak times, and quenching rates – thus motivating the need for a more sophisticated method of sorting the data and thus the shape-based grouping introduced in Section III.

Figure 3: 
UMAP projection of the sample of sSFHs reduced to two dimensions; the general shape of which we refer to as a “taco”. The layout and colours are the same as in Figure 1, though here the coloured points in the individual simulation panels indicate the galaxies from the respective simulation, overlaying the galaxies from the remaining sample in grey. Each point in the projection space represents one galaxy’s sSFH, as illustrated by the insets corresponding to highlighted points in the combined-simulations bottom-right panel. UMAP groups points in this space by how “similar” a given sSFH is to its neighbours based on the 136-dimensional sSFHs (corresponding to 136 simulation time steps) supplied to the algorithm. Thus, the horizontal and vertical axes are physically meaningless, and instead what is most informative is the clustering and spacing between points; two points close together represent galaxies with very similar sSFH profiles, with more distant points corresponding to distinct sSFH profiles. As a means to compare clusters of sSFHs, we have grouped the galaxies into 100 bins in this projection space in the style of a “battleship grid”, identifying individual bins by an alpha-numeric pair (e.g., D7). While there is some overlap between all simulations, there are certain regions of the taco dominated by certain (groups of) simulations, providing a hint into which sSFH profiles may be common amongst all simulations, and which may be unique to a given (group of) simulation(s). The goal of this paper is to describe common versus unique sSFH structure across all simulations.

Figure 4: Density of points in the UMAP projection space, computed from a normalized Gaussian KDE applied over the projection space, including only grid cells with at least 100 data points. The left panel shows the density evaluated on a $100\times 100$ mesh grid. The centre panel shows the same density averaged within each battleship-grid cell (value printed). The right panel shows each cell’s median sSFH (solid line) with its 16–84 percentile range (shading), coloured by the cell-averaged density. This three-panel layout – mesh or point-wise field, cell-averaged field, cell-median sSFH – is reused throughout the paper as a template for any quantity mapped onto the UMAP projection. The point distribution peaks in the centre of the taco and decreases radially. The per-cell sSFHs reveal three implicit projection axes (arrows): earlier peak time from left to right, stronger quenching along the A10 $\to$ J1 diagonal, and a steeper peak moving radially outward from the central high-density region.

Figure 5: The $z=0$ stellar mass ($M_{\star}$, top row) and specific star formation rate ($\dot{M}_{\star}/m_{\star}$, bottom row) of our galaxy sample, shown in the same three-panel layout as Figure 4 (individual points, cell log-average with values printed, and cell-median sSFH coloured by the cell-average). Both quantities vary smoothly along the A10 $\to$ J1 diagonal of the taco, with $M_{\star}$ increasing and $\dot{M}_{\star}/m_{\star}$ decreasing. Combining these trends with the implicit axes of Figure 4 shows the upper-right end of this diagonal corresponds to galaxies that assembled rapidly and quenched sharply, while the lower-left end corresponds to slow-assembling, still-star-forming galaxies. Ultimately, these trends are not surprising as present-day $\dot{M}_{\star}/m_{\star}$ is the final value of each sSFH, and SFH shape is known to correlate with stellar mass [88, 56].

Figure 6: Simulation-of-Origin Probabilities (SOPs, $P(\mathrm{sim}|\vec{x})$) – the conditional probability of any individual simulation producing an sSFH at point $\vec{x}$ in the projection space. Colours follow Figure 1, and the layout follows Figure 4. In the left panel, each point is coloured by the simulation with the highest SOP at its location, and filled contours trace increasing SOP values for that simulation, thus providing a map for the regions of the UMAP where each simulation dominates. The centre panel shows the largest cell-averaged-SOP (value printed) and thus provides insight into the distribution amongst simulations in a given cell: high probabilities mean galaxies from one simulation dominate the cell, while smaller probabilities correspond to a more-even spread amongst simulations. Insets show the full SOP distribution across all seven simulations for two example cells: C6 (the densest region of Figure 4) – strongly dominated by Illustris, and H1 – an edge cell with no clearly dominant simulation. The right panel shows the cell-median sSFH coloured by the dominant simulation.

Figure 7: Shannon entropy $H(\vec{x})$ of the SOP distribution across the UMAP: high $H(\vec{x})$ (yellow) highlights regions of commonality, corresponding to sSFHs frequently produced by most, if not all, simulations, while low $H(\vec{x})$ (indigo) shows regions of uniqueness exclusive to one or two simulations. The layout follows Figure 4, with filled contours in the left panel tracing increasing entropy. A broad “commonality strip” runs across the top of the taco, covering an arch from cells $\sim$B5 up to G2 and back down to J5; these cells correspond to the lowest maximum SOPs (i.e., fairest spread amongst simulations) in Figure 6. Likewise, the least common sSFHs amongst the simulations correspond to the largest maximum SOPs (i.e., cells dominated by a single simulation). The rarest sSFHs live in cells C6 and H5; C6 depicts a steady rise and long plateau, dominated by Illustris, and H5 shows near-immediate assembly followed by slow quenching, primarily produced by SC-SAM. Other semi-unique patches exist in cells C10 (including the D9 protrusion) – sSFHs characterized by a double peak, mainly occupied by SC-SAM, and D1 – steep, central peaks, primarily comprised of UM. Possible physical prescriptions likely to lead to these trends in commonality and uniqueness are discussed in Section V.

Figure 8: Per-cell comparison of the cell-averaged sSFHs in our $10\times 10$ UMAP binning against two assembly references. Top: reference curves for all halo masses, each divided by its median and coloured by $\log M_{h}$: the Behroozi et al. [5] average SFHs (left) and the Correa et al. [26] dark matter accretion histories $\dot{M}_{h}(t)$ (right). Bottom left: each cell’s median sSFH (solid black, with shaded grey $16$–$84$ percentile band) overplotted with the best-fitting Behroozi SFH at the inferred halo mass $M_{h}$, rescaled to the cell’s amplitude (the fit uses shape only). The Behroozi curve is coloured by $\log M_{h}$ where $\chi^{2}<1$ for the Behroozi and cell-averaged sSFH fit, and drawn as a dashed grey curve otherwise; each cell is annotated with its $\chi^{2}$. Bottom right: the same sSFHs overplotted with the Correa DMAH at the same inferred $M_{h}$, scaled to the sSFH amplitude and drawn in the matching colour where the Behroozi fit is good ($\chi^{2}<1$), as a dashed grey curve elsewhere; each cell is annotated with $\log M_{h}$. Cells shaded yellow have a high mean Shannon entropy ($\langle H(\vec{x})\rangle>2.3$; compare with Figure 7) and $\chi^{2}_{\rm SFH}<1$ to highlight the “commonality strip”. The inferred $M_{h}$ increases smoothly from the lower left to the upper right of the embedding, from $\log M_{h}\approx 9$–$11$ to $\approx 13$–$14.3$, consistent with the stellar-mass gradient of Figure 5; cells at $\log M_{h}=9$ sit at the lower edge of the Behroozi grid and should be read as limits. Low-$\chi^{2}$ cells concentrate in the commonality strip, where the Behroozi SFH at the inferred $M_{h}$ reproduces the cell’s shape well and the Correa DMAH shares its overall rise-and-fall form. Elevated values (up to $\chi^{2}\approx 2.4$) cluster along the sharply-quenched upper-right edge of the taco and in a few low-mass or double-peaked cells in the lower-left corner, where a smooth reference cannot capture such features. The commonality strip agreement anchors the “gravitational floor” argument developed in Section V.

Figure 9: Simulation-of-origin classification accuracy for the multi-objective autoencoder (Appendix C; left column) and the UMAP-based cell-argmax SOP classifier, which assigns each galaxy to the dominant simulation of its battleship cell (Figure 6; right column). Top row: confusion matrices, with true simulation in rows and predicted simulation in columns (rows normalized). The autoencoder reaches $\sim 95\%$ overall accuracy with a clean diagonal; Mufasa $\leftrightarrow$ Simba is the only substantial off-diagonal confusion. The SOP classifier reaches only $\sim 60$–$70\%$ and cannot predict Mufasa or Simba at all (hashed columns), because neither simulation dominates any battleship cell – they share their real estate with UniverseMachine, which “wins” the overlap in Figure 6. Bottom row: per-cell accuracy on the battleship grid. The autoencoder is uniformly accurate ($\geq 0.82$ in every populated cell), whereas the SOP classifier’s per-cell accuracy is structurally bounded by how cleanly a single simulation dominates each cell. The $\sim 25$–$30$ percentage-point gap anchors the argument in Section V: simulation-of-origin information in the sSFHs lives in more dimensions than a 2D UMAP can retain.

Figure 10: Milky Way analogues (MWAs) projected into the UMAP space, following a variant of the Figure 4 three-panel template. MWAs are selected via the $z=0$ $(M_{\star},\mathrm{SFR})$ criteria of Savelli et al. [103] (Appendix E) and weighted by a continuous “MW-ness” score $\gamma\in[0,1]$, with $\gamma=1$ matching the Milky Way’s observed values exactly. Left: every galaxy in the UMAP coloured and sized by $\gamma$ (more MW-like galaxies are bluer and have larger points, and galaxies very dissimilar from the MW are faint and orange). Centre: effective sample size $N=\sum_{i}\gamma_{i}$ per battleship cell (value printed). Right: cell-median sSFH for each cell, coloured by the cell’s $N$. MWAs occupy a broad band of the taco rather than a tight region, avoiding only the extreme low-mass, late-peaking corner (columns A–B, rows 8–10) and the extreme early-quenched corner (columns I–J, rows 1–2). MW-like $z=0$ $(M_{\star},\mathrm{SFR})$ is therefore reachable via a wide range of SFH morphologies, and the simulation-level spread within this band, rather than the band’s existence itself, is what distinguishes simulations at MW mass.

2610.17359.abstract: How galaxies assemble depends on processes ranging from small-scale baryonic physics to large-scale cosmological assembly, which are difficult to disentangle with observations alone. Using $\sim$63,000 simulated galaxies from seven cosmological simulations spanning hydrodynamical, semi-analytic, and semi-empirical models, we explore how specific star formation histories (sSFHs) vary across modelling assumptions. Using non-linear dimensionality reduction (UMAP), we find that sSFH shape variation organizes along a few smooth axes in a 2D embedding, broadly corresponding to (1) peak timing, (2) peak sharpness, and (3) subsequent quenching rate. We identify sSFH shapes that many simulations share ("common"), well described to first order by dark matter halo assembly, and a few tied to individual simulations ("unique"), which likely reflect subgrid and parametrization choices such as merger-triggered burst prescriptions. A notable exception is a common population of rapidly quenched galaxies found across most simulations, likely driven by e.g., active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback, that halo assembly alone cannot reproduce. The origin of the most distinctive unique shape, an Illustris-dominated history with an early peak and slow decline, remains unclear, but we test the effects of short-term variability. With a multi-objective auto-encoder neural network, we recover the simulation that a given sSFH is drawn from with $\sim$95\% out-of-sample accuracy; ablation tests indicate this information is embedded in long-timescale sSFH morphology rather than short-term variability. These results provide avenues for theoretical and observational follow-up connecting star formation histories to subgrid physical models.

2610.17390.abstract: Interstellar turbulence produces non-Gaussian polarized Galactic dust emission whose higher-order statistics depend on thermal phase and turbulent forcing. We synthesize optically thin dust polarization from three thermally multiphase diffuse interstellar medium (ISM) simulations with compressive, mixed, and solenoidal forcing. We characterize the resulting non-Gaussian structure in the warm, unstable, and cold phases using $E$- and $B$-mode spectra, one-point distributions, scale-dependent increments, and Minkowski functionals. Both $E$ and $B$ modes are intermittent. Warm-phase emission remains closest to Gaussian, whereas cold gas shows flatter intermediate-scale spectra, broader non-Gaussian tails, and the strongest departures from Gaussian morphology. Compressive forcing generally produces the strongest projected intermittency, particularly in the cold phase and total emission, while mixed and solenoidal forcing show weaker signatures. These higher-order structures also enhance spatial fluctuations in polarized dust power: Gaussian fields matched to the same two-point covariance underestimate the region-to-region scatter by factors of up to $\sim2.6$. Our results show that thermal phase and turbulent forcing regulate not only the mean polarized dust spectrum but also the field-to-field distribution of foreground power, with implications for modeling Galactic foreground in CMB polarization measurements.

2610.17556.abstract: Sulphur is drastically depleted from the gas phase in dense starless and prestellar cores, creating the long-standing "missing sulphur problem". Observations of sulphur-bearing molecules are crucial to understanding sulphur chemistry, core-environment relationships, and the physical evolution of star-forming regions. We present a survey of four sulphur-bearing molecules, HCS+, OCS, H2CS, and SO, towards 15 starless and prestellar cores in the Perseus molecular cloud using the Yebes 40m telescope. The HCS+ 1-0, OCS 3-2 and 4-3, H2CS 1_{0,1}-0_{0,0}, and SO 3_2-2_2 transitions were observed, fitted with Gaussian profiles, and column densities were calculated assuming local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE). We also compare these with observations of CS, CCS, and CCCS from a previous study. HCS+, OCS, H2CS, and SO are detected in 100%, 93%, 100%, and 73% of the sample, respectively. Derived column densities are (2.2-17.0)x10^11 cm^-2 for HCS+, (1.9-25.0)x10^12 cm^-2 for OCS, (1.0-15.0)x10^12 cm^-2 for H2CS, and (0.3-17.0)x10^13 cm^-2 for SO, spanning over an order of magnitude. HCS+ and SO abundances strongly correlate (inversely and directly, respectively) with core volume density, reinforcing their early- and late-type status. Correlations indicate a differentiation between carbon and oxygen chemistry for sulphur-bearing molecules, with CS showing the strongest correlations as expected. Cores in protostellar outflow paths do not show consistently higher abundances. The chemical age (SO/CS) correlates with physical age (volume density), except for Per752, an outlier likely linked to an enhanced cosmic ray ionization rate. These results provide a robust observational baseline constraining chemical models of sulphur chemistry in early star formation.

2610.17559.abstract: Little red dots (LRDs) are compact red sources at z>~4. Broad lines suggest accreting black holes, yet radio and X-ray measurements are usually weak. Local LRDs allow multi-frequency, multi-epoch radio studies that are inaccessible at high redshift. We search archival radio images for a counterpart to the local LRD J092359+415736 at z~0.323, quantify its long-term radio variability, and identify the plausible origin of the radio emission. Flux densities at the optical position are measured in FIRST, LoTSS, RACS, VAST, and VLASS products spanning 0.144-3.0 GHz and 1994-2024. A compact 144 MHz counterpart is detected at 42sigma in LoTSS, coincident with the Gaia position, and is recovered in FIRST, RACS, VAST, and VLASS. LoTSS and ASKAP give a spectral index alpha ~ -0.30 +/- 0.11. The source varies on multiple timescales: FIRST at 1.4 GHz (1994) is a factor of ~2.6 below ASKAP (2021-2024) and below the extrapolated LoTSS-ASKAP spectrum, indicating long-term brightening over 26 yr; the 3 GHz flux density rises by 2.3sigma between VLASS epochs 2.2 and 3.2. A star-formation-only origin would require ~200 Msun/yr, against an unobscured H-alpha upper limit of 3.3 Msun/yr, implying an extreme obscured starburst. Ordinary radio supernovae and tidal disruption events are strongly disfavoured by the luminosity and 30-yr recovery, while refractive scintillation would itself require an ultracompact nuclear emitter. The persistent radio counterpart is best explained by accretion onto the central black hole. Among the three radio-detected local LRDs, this source is intermediate in luminosity and the only one with reported multi-year variability, adding a temporal dimension to the radio diversity of the class.

2610.17575.abstract: Mergers are a crucial channel of galaxy growth, but their role relative to star formation remains uncertain at high redshift. Here we investigate merger rates and merger-driven stellar mass assembly for galaxies with stellar mass $M_\star \gtrsim 10^8 \, {\rm M_{\odot}}$ at $z\simeq 5-11$, by combining complementary theoretical approaches within $\Lambda$CDM. These include the DECODE semi-empirical model, the TNG100 and EAGLE hydrodynamical simulations, and the \textsc{L-Galaxies} semi-analytical model, together with the Millennium and TNG100-Dark simulations used to examine dark matter subhalo statistics and merger timescales. This compares models with different treatments of baryonic physics and galaxy-halo connections. We find that dark matter-only simulations predict merger timescales $\sim 30\%$ longer than those inferred from cosmological simulations including baryons. Galaxy major merger ($M_{\rm \star,sat} / M_{\rm \star,cen} > 0.25$) rates are high at cosmic dawn and increase towards earlier epochs, reaching $\sim 1/{\rm Gyr}$ at $z\sim 5$ and peaking at $\sim 3/{\rm Gyr}$ at $z\sim 8$. Despite these high rates, mergers contribute only $\lesssim 10\%$ of the total cosmic stellar mass density evolution. The ex-situ stellar mass fraction ranges from a few percent to $\sim 20\%$ for all galaxies at $z\gtrsim 5$, across different models and simulations. Their broad agreement implies that stellar mass assembly at cosmic dawn is dominated by in-situ star formation rather than mergers. These findings suggest that the high pair fractions identified by JWST may not directly trace efficient ex-situ stellar mass growth, highlighting the need for physically motivated merger timescales to interpret galaxy assembly in the early Universe.

The two most important coolants at all densities are shown with others made transparent for clarity. At all $Z$, dust-gas collisions ($\Lambda_{\rm gd}$) and continuum cooling processes ($\Lambda_{\rm cont}$) dominate at high $n$, and line cooling from chemical species at lower $n$. The species critical for cooling are CI/CII/OI fine-structure ($\Lambda_{\rm CI+CII+OI}$) and CO ($\Lambda_{\rm CO}$) at higher metallicities ($\gtrsim 0.1\rm Z_{\sun}$) whereas OH and $\rm H_{2}O$ cooling becomes critical at low $Z\lesssim 0.01\rm Z_{\sun}$ in dense gas. At the lowest $Z\lesssim 10^{-5}\rm Z_{\sun}$, there is a significant contribution from primordial species ($\Lambda_{\rm H_{2}}$, $\Lambda_{\rm HD}$). The transition from line to dust/gas continuum cooling occurs at increasingly higher $n$ at lower $Z$, implying that the gas temperature is sensitive to the chemical composition of the gas at low $Z$.

Figure 4: Column densities of various species as a function of $A_{\rm V}$ for the four PDR benchmark tests described in Röllig et al. [137]. Rows denote (from top to bottom): gas and dust temperatures, HI and $\mathrm{H_{2}}$, $\mathrm{C\,II}$, $\mathrm{C\,I}$, CO and $\rm e^{-}$ columns. The markers denote the values we obtain, and the lines in the background are results from PDR codes that participated in the benchmark: namely Cloudy [41], COSTAR [85, 86], HTBKW [159], KOSMA-$\tau$ [158, 11], Lee96mod [96], Leiden [17, 161], Meijerink [103], Meudon [95], Sternberg [155, 156], and UCL_PDR [10].
Figure 5: Continuation of Figure 4. Rows denote (from top to bottom): column density of $\rm H_{3}^{+}$, OH, CH, and $\mathrm{O\,I}$.

Figure 6: Thermochemical state of gas in supersonically turbulent patches at different metallicities (columns), as described in Section IV.1. The top row shows the mass-weighted average gas temperature ($T_{\mathrm{gas}}$) and the following rows show column densities of $\mathrm{H_{2}}$, CI, CO, OH, and $\rm H_{2}O$. We can see the expected evolution with $Z$ and highlight the presence of $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ gas at low $Z$, which is better traced by CI and OH than CO.

Figure 7: Average properties of the gas as a function of total hydrogen nuclei density ($n_{\rm Hnuclei}$) compared for the four $Z$, with shaded region showing the 1-$\sigma$ variation at that density. Panels show the volume-weighted PDFs (top-left), gas temperature ($T_{\mathrm{gas}}$; top-middle), fine-structure cooling rates (top-right), abundances of $\mathrm{H\,I}$ and $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ (bottom-left), of $\mathrm{C\,I}$, $\mathrm{C\,II}$ and $\mathrm{O\,I}$ (bottom-middle) and of molecular species CO, OH and $\rm H_{2}O$ (bottom-right).

Figure 8: Relevant quantities compared for a HII regions/PDR in a $\sim 100\,\rm pc$ turbulent patch at different gas-phase $Z$, driven by a UV source ($\sim 1000\rm M_{\sun}$ star cluster). The rows show slices of gas temperature ($T_{\mathrm{gas}}$), number densities of electrons ($n_{\rm e}$), $\mathrm{H\,I}$ ($n_{\rm HI}$), the gas thermal pressure ($P_{\rm therm}/k_{\rm B}$), the photoelectric heating rate ($\Gamma_{\rm PE}$) and the ratio of OI and CII fine-structure cooling rates.

Figure 9: Radial profiles of gas temperature $T_{\mathrm{gas}}$ (solid) and dust temperature $T_{\rm dust}$ (dashed, top panel), and total hydrogen nuclei number density $n$ (bottom panel), at $t\sim 10\,\rm Myr$ for the turbulent $\mathrm{H\,II}$ region/PDR calculation described in Section IV.2, for the four metallicities considered. Lines show the azimuthal median and shaded regions the $1\sigma$ scatter at fixed radius. The ionization front, marked by the sharp drop in $T_{\mathrm{gas}}$ and the compressed density shell in the bottom panel, occurs at progressively larger and less well-defined radii as $Z$ decreases, as the associated density shell weakens and eventually disappears by $Z=10^{-4}\rm Z_{\sun}$, reflecting the reduced ability of the swept-up gas to cool and compress at low $Z$.

Figure 10: 2D histograms of the line integrated column density distributions of CO and $\mathrm{C\,I}$ with respect to $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ obtained in the turbulent patch simulations presented in Section IV.1. Solid black line indicates the bi$n$ed-average trend of this obtained distribution from the simulation, which can be compared with the dashed line that shows the outcome of a corresponding static 1D PDR with the same average nn and radiation/CR background as the simulation (see Section V.1). Markers indicate a compilation of UV absorption line measurements of these species in the diffuse ISM [129, 146, 180, 21]. We can see that our simulations are able to simultaneously reproduce observed $\mathrm{C\,I}$ and CO columns, whereas the corresponding static model overestimates $\mathrm{C\,I}$ columns.

2610.17577.abstract: We present a flexible implementation of non-equilibrium chemical networks with the $\texttt{KROME}$ framework, coupled to a nonlocal variable Eddington tensor-closed radiation transport scheme ($\texttt{VETTAM}$). Our fiducial network is designed to explicitly capture the formation pathways of important molecular species such as CO, OH, and $\rm H_2O$, intermediaries like $\rm H_3^+$, and the destruction of these species through photon and cosmic-ray dissociation. We validate our scheme through benchmark tests, and demonstrate its success in 1D and 3D problems covering a broad range of metallicities ($0 \leq Z \lesssim \rm Z_{\odot}$) and densities ($n \lesssim 10^{17} \, \rm cm^{-3}$). We confirm earlier works that suggest that OH and $\rm H_2O$ are the key molecular species in dense gas ($n \gtrsim 10^{5} \, \rm cm^{-3}$) for $Z\lesssim 0.01 \rm Z_{\odot}$, dominate the cooling at these densities, and demonstrate that our scheme can reproduce their abundances with similar accuracy as dedicated static photo-dissociation region (PDR) codes. We also find that the dominant fine-structure coolant in dense ($n \gtrsim 10^3 \, \, \rm cm^{-3}$) PDRs transitions from CI to CII to OI at increasingly lower $Z$. Finally, we find that in turbulent media, rapid mixing at PDR interfaces renders the chemical species out of equilibrium, and show that this could potentially alleviate the long-standing problem of (static) PDR models producing excess CI in the diffuse ISM over UV absorption-line measurements. We conclude by presenting and comparing with alternative implementations of reduced but faster chemical networks in our scheme, discussing the problem-dependent performance-accuracy tradeoffs and future prospects.
