2610.17753.abstract: We investigate the thermal phase structures and kinematics of atomic hydrogen (H I) gas in the Draco nebula to clarify how infalling H I evolves toward cold atomic and molecular clouds. Using the DHIGLS H I 21 cm data, we apply the Regularized Optimization for Hyper-Spectral Analysis (ROHSA) algorithm to decompose the emission into spatially coherent Gaussian components, and classify them as warm neutral medium (WNM), lukewarm neutral medium (LNM), and cold neutral medium (CNM). We identify two kinematically distinct WNM components: WNM1 near $-3$ km s$^{-1}$ and WNM2 near $-30$ km s$^{-1}$. The LNM forms a broad velocity bridge between two WNMs, whereas the CNM is concentrated within a narrower intermediate velocity range. CO emission is also confined to this interval and is associated with CNM-rich regions. The H I mass fractions are $\sim 41\%$, $\sim 23\%$, $\sim 17\%$, and $\sim 19\%$ for WNM1, WNM2, LNM, and CNM, respectively, with the LNM and CNM together accounting for $\sim 36\%$ of the total H I mass. No comparably independent WNM component is recovered at intermediate velocities, although a weak broad component may remain unresolved. The observed phase structures are consistent with a dynamically compressed multiphase interaction layer in which compression increases the gas density, shortens the radiative cooling time, and drives the evolution from WNM through thermally unstable gas toward the CNM. The present interaction may both create new CNM, and further compress or grow pre-existing dense structures. Our results provide the missing link between previous evidence for dynamical interaction and molecular cloud formation in Draco, and identify CNM formation as a key step in transforming gas accreting toward the Galactic disk into cold atomic and molecular clouds.

2610.18046.title: Atomic hydrogen in $z=0$ galaxies in the COLIBRE simulations

figures.caption: Figure 1: Examples of H i discs from the COLIBRE L025m5 run ‘observed’ similarly to the highest-resolution (r00_t00) reduction of MHONGOOSE survey data from MeerKAT: $8\,\mathrm{arcsec}$ and $1\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ resolution, $1\,\mathrm{deg}$ field of view and column density sensitivity of $10^{19.8}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ at $3\sigma$ over $16\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ – further details are given in Appendix B. The upper panels (A) show a giant galaxy and the lower panels (B) a dwarf – note the different spatial scales shown in the second column; further properties of the galaxies are given in Table 1. Both are seen $\approx 60\,\mathrm{deg}$ inclined. In each group of panels (A & B) the upper row shows from left to right: mock HST image with limiting surface brightness of $1\,\mathrm{L}_{\odot}\,\mathrm{pc}^{-2}$ and H i column density contour at $10^{19.8}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$; H i column density map; first moment map (intensity-weighted mean velocity) centred on the systemic velocity of the disc; second moment map (intensity-weighted velocity dispersion). The second row zooms in to show only the primary source, masked in 3D, and adds contours to the moment maps. The small red point in the box in the second panel shows the beam size. The outermost column density contour repeats the contour in the left panel; additional contours are spaced by factors of $4$. Velocity contours are spaced by $50$ and $15\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, respectively. Velocity dispersion contours are at $12$, $24$ and $36\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The giant galaxy has a regularly rotating disc with a small central hole (see Sec. 3.2.7) and dense clouds reaching $N_{\mathrm{HI}}\approx 10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$. Much of the disc has a velocity dispersion of $\approx 15\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, but there are numerous local patches exceeding $30\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The disc is surrounded by small clouds out to $>100\,\mathrm{kpc}$ broadly co-rotating with the disc (see Sec. 3.2.8). 2610.18046.abstract: We present an overview of the properties of atomic hydrogen (HI) in galaxies at redshift $z=0$ in the COLIBRE cosmological galaxy formation simulations. COLIBRE directly simulates the multi-phase interstellar medium (ISM) and includes new methods to follow radiative cooling to $\approx 10\,\rm{K}$, non-equilibrium chemistry coupled to dust, and dust formation, growth \& destruction. We focus on the $(200\,\rm{cMpc})^3$ volume with resolution elements of $2\times 10^{6}\,\rm{M}_{\odot}$. No HI properties informed the calibration of model parameters and yet we find very good agreement with the observed $M_{\star}$-$M_{\rm{HI}}$ relation, the HI mass and velocity width functions, the HI mass-size relation, and (baryonic) Tully-Fisher relations, albeit with some mismatches at the extremes of the galaxy population. HI surface density profiles are realistic, except at large radii around massive ($M_{\star}\gtrsim 10^{10}\,\rm{M}_{\odot}$) galaxies where we find a population of possibly spurious circumgalactic HI clouds, whose abundances and masses decrease, however, with increasing mass resolution). Using smaller simulations to vary some of the uncertain model parameters, we find that the main scaling relations are at most mildly affected, although this may not extend to detailed HI morphokinematics. Convergence across mass resolution levels a factor of $8$ higher and lower is good: the median HI mass and HI `occupation fraction' as a function of halo mass, and the HI mass function, are remarkably stable, although the highest resolution model overproduces HI sources by a factor of $\approx2$ at $M_{\rm{HI}}\gtrsim 3\times 10^{9}\,\rm{M}_{\odot}$. Upturns in the low-mass and low-velocity slopes of the HI mass and velocity width functions with potentially subtle observational signatures are predicted.

2610.18099.abstract: Extended diffuse radio emission in the central regions of galaxy clusters is commonly associated with non-thermal processes in the intracluster medium (ICM), but its origin and the mechanisms responsible for sustaining it remain uncertain. We present the discovery and multi-wavelength analysis of two diffuse radio sources, MKTJ0355-4237 and MKTJ0355-4230, to assess their nature and investigate their radio spectral and magnetic field properties through radio polarimetric analysis. We use deep MeerKAT L-band (1.28 GHz) observations to perform spectral analysis of the diffuse emission and study its polarisation properties via rotation measure synthesis. These are complemented by eROSITA X-ray data and DESI photometric redshift catalogues to characterise the host cluster environments. MKTJ0355-4237 is confirmed as cluster-scale minihalo with extent of $\sim 400$ kpc, while the other diffuse source MKTJ0355-4230 remain uncertain and could be either associated with a radio minihalo or radio tailed galaxy. Both show steep spectra ($\alpha \approx -0.7$ to $-0.8$) that steepen toward the outskirts ($\alpha \lesssim -2.5$), consistent with spatial variations in electron ageing and re-acceleration. Polarised emission is detected in both systems, with fractional polarisation $\sim1\,\%$ in the centres and increasing in the outer regions of MKTJ0355-4237. MKTJ0355-4230 is associated with a previously uncatalogued cluster and shows an X-ray morphology offset from the brightest cluster galaxy, indicative of dynamical activity. MKTJ0355-4237 exhibits a sharply bounded internal radio deficit without a corresponding X-ray counterpart, within current sensitivity limits. The spectral steepening supports turbulent re-acceleration as the origin of the diffuse emission.

2610.18263.abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope has unlocked uncharted territory for the study of early black holes, enabling the detection of fainter and smaller black holes at larger cosmological distances than previously possible. Compared to nearby massive black holes, they are characterised by several unexpected attributes, such as their multi-wavelength properties or their relation to their host galaxies. These observational findings challenge our understanding of the past evolution of present-day supermassive black holes, and provide novel anchor points to constrain theoretical models of black hole formation and growth. This review summarises our current understanding of the observed properties of newly discovered, active black holes in the early Universe, discusses the status of mass measurements and the relation to their hosts, as well as open questions and future prospects.

2610.18282.abstract: (Abridged) Baryonic feedback is expected to transform cuspy dark-matter (DM) haloes into cores, but direct observational links between inner DM slopes and galaxy star-formation histories (SFHs) remain limited. We investigate and quantify the connection between halo inner slopes and baryonic assembly histories in a large sample of intermediate-z galaxies. We analyse 375 galaxies at 0.1<z<1.43 spanning 7<log(Mstar/Msun)<11.2 using 3D forward modelling of MUSE kinematics and disk-halo decompositions with mass-dependent (DC14-based) and generalised Navarro-Frenk-White (gNFW) halo profiles. Stellar population parameters are inferred from multi-band Spectral Energy Distribution fitting of UV-to-MIR photometry using a non-parametric SFH model. Bayesian model comparison shows that the DC14-based halo density profiles are statistically preferred over gNFW for a substantial fraction of the sample. The inferred inner slopes from gNFW fits nevertheless follow the DC14 expectation and reproduce the expected dependence on the stellar-to-halo mass ratio, despite this not being explicitly imposed. Partial correlation coefficient and random forest regression analyses consistently identify stellar mass (or, equivalently, the stellar-to-halo mass ratio) as the primary driver of the inner density slope, a result that holds robustly even when the analysis is restricted to the gNFW fits. In contrast, SFH-related quantities (e.g. formation time and 'burstiness' indicators) exhibit no independent predictive power on the DM halo inner slope once the dependence on stellar mass is accounted for. Cored systems preferentially occupy lower-mass, more bursty bins with later assembly times, whereas cuspy systems are associated with higher stellar masses, lower star formation activity, and earlier assembly epochs, in agreement with theoretical expectations of stellar-feedback-induced cores.

2610.18285.abstract: We present an Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) radio-continuum detection of the nearby spiral Seyfert I type galaxy NGC 7213 which we nickname `Sand-timer' due to its morphological appearance. We find intriguing, peculiar emission extending from the central supermassive black hole (SMBH), which we refer to as galaxy hyperbubbles and/or active galactic nucleus (AGN) jets. Finally, we find two previously undetected kiloparsec-scale features in the polarised intensity image, which appear most likely also related to the central SMBH, as restarted bipolar radio jets, though somewhat obscured in the radio-continuum total intensity image. They resemble the bow shocks often seen in Fanaroff-Riley Class II (FR-II) radio galaxies, and so we propose they most likely represent an early episode of the `Sand-timer's' AGN jet activity. An alternative scenario is that the core of NGC 7213 may be a supermassive binary black hole (SMBBH) undergoing a tidal disruption event (TDE), potentially causing the peculiar radio-continuum emission.

2610.18473.abstract: In galaxies, stellar populations represent a superposition of both in situ and accreted components, tracing internal chemical evolution as well as the histories of merged satellites. We investigate how assembly history shapes the chemical properties of present-day stellar populations in low-mass dwarf galaxies. We analyze a suite of EDGE-INFERNO star-by-star cosmological zoom-in simulations of galaxies with present-day halo mass $\sim1.4\times10^9\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$. We systematically vary galaxy growth while preserving the present-day halo mass, engineering our simulations to span a continuum of assembly histories. Early-forming systems form most of their stars in a single progenitor, with centrally concentrated star formation and a continuous enrichment history. In contrast, our late-forming systems assemble by accretion of multiple progenitors with their own stellar populations, resulting in fragmented star formation across several halos with independent chemical evolution tracks. These regimes produce qualitatively different chemical signatures: single-progenitor systems exhibit connected, well-defined trends in abundance space, while multi-progenitor systems show multiple, distinct stellar populations with limited overlap. We find that metallicity distribution functions provide initial constraints on assembly history for samples of at least $50$-$100$ member stars. Multi-element abundance analysis significantly improves the recovery of distinct components, although robust reconstruction still requires larger samples. Fully separating in situ and accreted populations likely requires kinematic information. Accreted stars can contribute substantially even at high metallicities in multi-progenitor systems, while external enrichment can cause accreted material to follow similar chemical trends as in situ stars, particularly in the single-progenitor regime.

2610.18505.abstract: We review the accretion-driven channel of stellar black-hole growth and spin-up in gaseous star clusters, developed within the framework of our MSCA project "protoBH". Our detailed calculations involving semi-analytic modelling, dynamical and hydrodynamic simulations suggest that the growth and spin-up of initially low-mass stellar black holes is an integral element of the formation process of dense massive star clusters, such as the proto-globular clusters observed at high redshift. The black holes accrete residual gas, remaining from the first star formation event, and form accretion disks generated by gas angular momentum induced by the black-holes' own curved orbits. Assuming initial black hole masses below the pair-instability mass gap $\leq 55\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, the gap gets populated with black-hole masses growing to $\sim 10^2\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, and even reaching several hundred solar masses for sufficiently dense and massive proto-clusters. We predict a consistent spin-mass relation with low black hole spins $\lesssim 0.2$ for low black hole masses $\lesssim 20\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, spanning all intermediate spins for higher masses and saturating to high spins $\gtrsim 0.8$ for high masses $\gtrsim 70\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$. We find evidence in favour of such an accretion-driven subpopulation of black holes in the GWTC-5.0 released by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration.

2610.18576.abstract: The massive disk galaxies (stellar mass >= 10^11 M_solar ) in the local universe (z < 0.1) encode challenging aspects of galaxy formation physics. We have studied one class of such galaxies - the giant low surface brightness galaxies (gLSBs) that show a hybrid morphology - a central Sersic, an inner high surface brightness, exponential stellar disk surrounded by an outer, extended low surface brightness disk, using large volume IllustrisTNG-100 simulation. This is motivated by the recent observation of several such systems and an earlier work by Sarkar & Saha (2025) from IllustrisTNG-50. We find that despite using a ~ 10 times larger volume simulation, only ~11% of massive disk galaxies show such morphology, consistent with findings from TNG50. This shows robustly that such galaxies are not common in the local universe. We compared them with the typical disk galaxies from observations, and single-exponential gLSBs from TNG100. We show that while the inner disk components lie well within the central surface brightness vs. radial scale length distribution of the typical disks, the outer LSB disks lie significantly at the outskirt, occupying a unique space. Their median bulge-to-total ratio is ~ 0.2 making them disk dominated, similar to the typical disks and the single-exponential gLSBs. We find their median dark matter mass fraction to be high (~ 0.9), typical of gLSBs. The outer LSB disks reach fainter central surface brightness and larger scale length values than the single-exponential gLSBs. Our exploration will be useful in understanding their formation mechanism across cosmic time.

2610.18601.abstract: Dormant black holes (dormant BHs, i.e., X-ray quiet binaries comprising a BH and a companion star) are probes of the effect of cluster dynamics and binary stellar evolution on compact-object binaries. A dozen dormant BH binaries are known, a number that will increase substantially with the upcoming Gaia Data Release 4 (DR4). Their origin is uncertain, and dynamical formation is proposed as one possible channel. Here, we study the formation of dormant BHs in low-mass star clusters, accounting for the interplay of binary stellar evolution and cluster dynamics. We present new simulations with the $N$-body code PeTar, interfaced with the population synthesis code SEVN for single and binary star evolution. Our grid spans a range of cluster masses ($300-4800\,$M$_\odot$), metallicities ($1.4\times10^{-2}$, $1.4\times10^{-4}$), and natal kick models (with and without fallback). We find that almost all dormant BH binaries escape the parent cluster within $\sim1\,$Gyr ($\sim10\,$Myr) when assuming weak (strong) natal kicks. Most ($73\%$) dormant BHs form via the exchange of a BH (or its progenitor star) into a stellar binary, or of a star into a binary with a BH. Dormant BHs in low-mass clusters have a wide orbital period distribution (from a few hours to $10^8\,$d), with an upper limit set by natal kicks, a bimodal eccentricity distribution (a first peak at zero eccentricity for circularised systems and a second at high eccentricity), and stellar masses that follow the (evolved) initial mass function. Large BH masses are a smoking gun of dynamical formation, via exchanges and stellar collisions. We expect Gaia DR4 to contain $\sim1-64$ high-metallicity and $\sim0.4-48$ low-metallicity dormant BHs, with a period distribution peaking at $\sim10^3\,$d, $\gtrsim90\%$ of them with eccentricity $e>0.1$, and $\sim20\%$ with large BH masses ($m_{\rm BH} \gtrsim 30\,$M$_\odot$).

2610.18648.abstract: We present the first deep, targeted LOFAR 144 MHz source catalogue of the COSMOS field, together with the first 144 MHz source counts in this field. The data comprise 48 h of observations. Over the 2.6 sq. deg. region adopted for the catalogue analysis, the final Dutch-array image reaches a median rms sensitivity of ~100 uJy/beam at an angular resolution of 15" x 6". The resulting catalogue contains 1984 radio sources; a peak S/N >= 5 selection is adopted for the resolved/unresolved classification and source-count analysis. We characterised the catalogue using Monte Carlo source-injection and recovery simulations, including dedicated simulations of extended sources, to quantify completeness, flux-density redistribution, and morphology-dependent source-recovery effects. The catalogue reaches 90% completeness at 1.48 mJy. The resulting Euclidean-normalised differential source counts are measured down to ~0.4 mJy and show good agreement with LoTSS DR3 144 MHz source counts and with the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz counts scaled to 144 MHz, with ~5% of catalogue sources having multiple 3 GHz counterparts within a beam-matched search region. Comparison with the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz catalogue shows good astrometric agreement, with median offsets of Delta_RA = 0.35" (+0.03"/-0.05") and Delta_Dec = -0.83" (+0.02"/-0.03"), approximately 6% of the corresponding synthesised-beam dimensions, and no significant radial dependence across the field. The resulting catalogue provides a low-frequency view of COSMOS and a reference dataset for future deeper LOFAR observations and multiwavelength studies of this extensively characterised extragalactic field.

2610.18659.title: The Connection Between the Growth of Massive Black Holes and Their Dynamical Histories

figures.caption: Figure 1: The stellar mass - black hole mass relation as a function of number of main progenitor branch mergers. The accreted (top row) and total (bottom row) masses of central MBHs are plotted against the stellar masses of their host galaxies, with points coloured by the total number of MBH mergers occurring along the main progenitor branch. The left and right columns show Romulus25 and RomulusC, respectively. The red shaded region shows the best-fitting relation between accreted or total MBH mass and stellar mass for galaxies with $M_{\rm stell}>10^{9},{\rm M_{\odot}}$, with the shaded region corresponding to $\pm 2\sigma$ about the best fit. In the top panels, we classify central MBHs lying below the shaded region as under-grown relative to their host galaxy. The number of mergers generally increases along the relation, however, under-grown central MBHs have lower merger counts compared with the general, more massive population at a given host galaxy stellar mass. This suggests that the accretion history of a MBH is related to its merger history. The blue line shows the observed stellar mass - black hole mass relation of Schramm and Silverman (2013).

Figure 2: Distribution of ex-situ accretion among MBHs. The normalised distributions of the fraction of a black hole’s accreted mass which has been accreted ex-situ for the most massive, central black holes in galaxies for the field (red; Romulus25) and cluster (blue; RomulusC) environments. The distributions are highly similar, with both displaying peaks at zero and quickly dropping for higher fractions.

Figure 3: Comparison of the ex-situ growth for MBHs for different stellar mass bins in the field and cluster populations. The normalised distributions of the fraction of a black hole’s total accretion which is ex-situ for the most massive central black holes in galaxies in the field (solid; Romulus25) and cluster (dashed; RomulusC) environments, divided into four host galaxy stellar mass bins. The distributions are similar in both environments, with the three lower stellar mass bins displaying peaks at zero and the highest stellar mass bin peaking at a higher fraction of approximately 0.2. higher stellar mass bins also display wider distributions than the lower mass bins. MBHs typically gain most of their mass from in-situ accretion regardless of mass or environment.

Figure 4: The stellar mass - black hole mass relations and the fraction of time a MBH spends at galaxy centre. The accreted mass of central MBHs are plotted against the stellar mass of their host galaxies, with data points coloured by the fraction of its lifetime that a black hole has spent in the central 700 pc of its current host galaxy, $f_{\rm cen}$. The red and blue shaded regions show the $M_{\rm BH}-M_{\rm stell}$ scaling relations for early- and late- type galaxies, respectively, from Greene et al. (2020). For the Romulus25 population, $f_{\rm cen}$ is typically high, above approximately 70% for data points on or near the relation. However, for under-grown MBHs below the relation, the fraction is lower than their counterparts in similar mass galaxies. For the RomulusC population, a similar but much weaker trend is seen.

Figure 5: Examples of three archetypical dynamical evolution scenarios leading to under-grown MBHs. The ratio of a black hole’s accretion rate to host galaxy star formation rate versus time, traced along the black hole’s main progenitor branch (red) and along the final host galaxy’s main progenitor branch (blue). Each panel is labelled with final MBH accreted mass and host stellar mass. Each MBH is under-grown compared to the general population at the same galaxy mass. Each of the under-grown MBHs in the field environment display one of the types of evolutions shown. For the top right and bottom left panels, no data is shown for the last ~2 Gyr, and for the centre top and middle panels there are gaps seen at ~5 Gyr, in each case this is due to the galaxy SFR being 0. In all scenarios shown, the MBH spends the majority of its lifetime accreting at substantially lower values than what would be required to exist on typical scaling relations.

Figure 6: Examples of growth histories for MBHs that have typical masses. The ratio of MBH accretion rate to host galaxy SFR over time, tracking along the MBH’s main progenitor branch (red) and the galaxy’s main progenitor branch (blue). Mass matched examples from Romulus25 to the galaxies presented in Fig. 5 selected to have more typical final accreted masses. While co-evolutiom is the most common evolutionary path (left), we find examples of ‘late entrance’ and ‘competing’ MBHs, but these phases end much earlier than the under-grown population.

Figure 7: Some galaxies with under-grown MBHs have more massive wandering MBHs in them. The relation between the total MBH accreted mass for central, under-grown MBHs and their host galaxy stellar mass is shown in red stars. Arrows are drawn between them and the most massive, wandering MBHs (blue circle) in the same galaxy. Only two galaxies in this sample have an off-centre MBH with an accreted mass substantially closer to the empirical relation.

Figure 8: Two examples of galaxies that have their most massive MBHs off-centre. Top: a galaxy with a wanderer that has a typical accreted mass for its galaxy’s stellar mass. Bottom: an example where the off-centre MBH is still substantially under-grown by $z=0$. In each panel we follow the MBH that is the most massive, central MBH at $z=0$ (red), the MBH that is the most massive in the entire galaxy at $z=0$ (blue), and the most central MBH along the galaxy’s main progenitor branch (green, dashed). The left column shows the ratio of the MBH accretion rate to the host galaxy SFR as a function of time. The middle column shows the evolution of accreted MBH mass with host galaxy stellar mass. The right column shows the distance of each MBH from the centre of its host galaxy as a function of time. The galaxy merger that brings the two $z=0$ MBHs into the same host is indicated by a vertical black line in the left and right panels at the time of the merger, and by black stars along their evolutionary tracks in the middle panels. Apparent sudden decreases in stellar mass in the middle panels occur during galaxy mergers, when the halo finder can briefly reassign particles between the merging halos.

2610.18659.abstract: Massive black holes (MBHs) grow through both gas accretion and mergers and it remains unclear how variations to MBH growth and dynamical histories contribute to the spread in empirical scaling relations between MBHs and their host galaxies. We examine the ex- and in-situ growth of MBHs within large-scale cosmological simulations and compare the evolution of an outlier population of under-grown MBHs to the general population. We use the Romulus25 uniform volume cosmological simulation and the RomulusC cluster zoom-in simulation to examine the growth and merger histories of MBHs. We identify central MBHs that are undergrown relative to other MBHs in similar mass galaxies and investigate their accretion, merger, and orbital histories within the simulations. The contribution of ex-situ growth increases with MBH mass, with mergers becoming increasingly important in the most massive galaxies. We find no difference between cluster and field environments in terms of the importance of ex-situ growth, which is generally very low. Under-grown MBHs have experienced fewer mergers and have had complex dynamical histories, spending significant time 'drifting' within the galaxy or 'competing' with another MBH. Other under-grown MBHs have experienced a 'late entrance' into a galaxy which until then had no central MBH. Our results demonstrate that MBH assembly is dominated by in-situ growth, which in turn is impacted by the dynamical histories of MBHs within assembling galaxies. Prolonged off-centre evolution can suppress accretion and contribute to the formation of under-grown central MBHs at $z=0$.

2610.14166.abstract: Gaia has substantially expanded the sample of candidate white dwarfs (WDs) in open clusters, but many remain without spectroscopic characterization. We leverage the increasingly extensive archives of large public spectroscopic surveys to identify 62 candidate cluster WDs with available spectra from DESI, LAMOST, and SDSS. After discarding sources with very low S/N and unreliable host clusters, 44 candidates remain, including 37 non-magnetic DA WDs, of which 15 had not previously been characterized in the literature for cluster studies. We find that nine are consistent with single-star origins in their proposed host clusters, increasing the combined cluster DA initial--final mass relation (IFMR) sample to 132 WDs. All lie within $2\sigma$ of the best-fit IFMR from the most comprehensive recent cluster WD sample, suggesting these additions do not require recalibrating the empirical IFMR. One is a likely Hyades tidal-tail WD, providing further evidence that dynamical dispersal helps explain the long-standing WD deficit in the nearest cluster. We further compare WDs with spectra from multiple surveys. Among seven Praesepe WDs observed by both DESI and SDSS, DESI gives higher WD masses in six cases, with a mean difference of $0.067\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, while the inferred progenitor masses differ by as much as $0.459\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$. More broadly, nine of ten single-star cluster DAs with DESI spectra lie above the empirical IFMR, with a mean final-mass residual of $0.06\pm0.04\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$. These results show that survey-dependent differences can strongly affect cluster WD parameters, and should be considered when combining heterogeneous spectroscopy in empirical IFMR studies.

2610.14167.title: Where Cluster Galaxies Reside and How Strongly They Lens

figures.caption: Figure 1: Environmental impact on member lensing strength for an Inert Member, a Boosted Lens, and an Intrinsic Lens: each is modeled as a singular isothermal sphere in a uniform, subcritical external convergence and shear field, for illustration. Top panels show the tangential critical curves in isolation (blue dashed) and with the cluster environment included (orange solid). The environmental shear distorts the otherwise circular critical curves. Gray dotted circles mark the reference radius $\theta_{\rm ref}=0\farcs 5$. Their intersections with unity give the corresponding Einstein radii, marked by triangles and diamonds. The first two members have identical isolated profiles, but the stronger environment in the middle column raises $\theta_{\rm E,cl}$ above the reference radius. The rightmost member is critical even in isolation. The annotated boost is $\mathcal{B}=\theta_{\rm E,cl}/\theta_{\rm E,iso}$.

The dashed line at unity indicates agreement. The left panel indicates the fractions of members where the cluster environment is already critical. The middle panel shows the Major and Minor Perturber fractions among members in the cluster-critical region, while the right panel shows the Intrinsic Lens, Boosted Lens, and Inert Member fractions among members in cluster-subcritical regions. Filled circles and vertical intervals give the cluster-balanced median and 16th–84th percentiles across the 60 analogs. Downward triangles mark ratios below the plotted range.

$\theta_{E,\rm iso}\geq x$, normalized within that population. The bottom row shows the fraction with cluster-field Einstein radius $\theta_{E,\rm cl}\geq x$. Contributions are separated into Intrinsic Lenses, Boosted Lenses, and Inert Members. The reference scale $\theta_{\rm ref}=0.5\arcsec$ marks the adopted GGSL threshold. Relative to the simulations, the observed clusters contain more members with large isolated lensing strength and a larger population that exceeds the GGSL threshold after the local cluster field is included. The class decomposition shows that this difference is driven primarily by the larger observed populations of Intrinsic and Boosted Lenses.

Figure 5: Subhalo mass distributions separated by lensing class: the left panel shows the selected members of the six observed clusters, while the right panel shows one TNG-Cluster analog for each observed cluster, chosen as the closest match in primary Einstein radius $\theta_{\rm E,p}$. Histograms are divided by lensing class: Intrinsic Lenses, Boosted Lenses, Major Perturbers, Minor Perturbers, and Inert Members. The overall subhalo-mass distributions are similar in the observed and simulated samples, but their lensing classifications differ at fixed mass. Observed clusters contain a larger fraction of Intrinsic and Boosted Lenses, whereas simulated members of comparable mass are more often classified as Inert. This shows that the discrepancy is not primarily driven by a deficit of massive subhalos, but by differences in their lensing efficiency at fixed mass.

Figure 6: Member abundance and lensing strength as a function of local cluster environment:
the left column shows the observed clusters and the right column their matched TNG-Cluster analogs. The top row gives the number of members in bins of environmental strength, parameterized by $\kappa_{\rm env}+\gamma_{\rm env}$, with colors indicating lensing class. The middle and bottom rows show, respectively, the summed cluster-field Einstein radii, $\theta_{E,\rm cl}$, and summed isolated Einstein radii, $\theta_{\rm E,iso}$, contributed by members in each bin. The upper horizontal axis gives the median projected cluster-centric radius of members in each environmental bin, illustrating the correspondence between stronger local lensing fields and smaller projected radii. Compared with the simulations, the observed clusters place more members in the strongest environments and contain greater galaxy-scale lensing strength across the subcritical regime, particularly from Intrinsic and Boosted Lenses.

Figure 7: 
Changes in lensing-class caused by line-of-sight structure: colored regions show the cluster-balanced fraction of baseline Inert Members that become Boosted Lenses or Minor Perturbers after the line-of-sight planes are included. Figure 8: The first panel shows the fraction of dark-matter mass transferred from the tNFW envelope to the Plummer component as a function of subhalo mass. The solid curve and shaded band show the median and 16th–84th percentiles from 1,000 bootstrap refits. The second panel shows the dark matter density profile of a representative member before and after the response. 2610.14167.abstract: The efficiency of galaxy-galaxy strong lensing (GGSL) in clusters depends jointly on the inner mass distributions of member galaxies and their locations within the cluster potential. Observed GGSL probabilities exceed $\Lambda$CDM predictions by nearly an order of magnitude, but the relative roles of internal structure and environment remain unclear. We disentangle these effects by comparing HST strong-lensing clusters with TNG-Cluster analogs at similar lens redshifts, matched by their primary Einstein radius. For each member, we measure its lensing strength in isolation and when embedded in the cluster field. Members in cluster-critical regions are classified as Major or Minor Perturbers depending on whether they strongly lens in isolation; those in subcritical regions are classified as Intrinsic Lenses, Boosted Lenses, or Inert Members according to whether they lens independently, only with environmental assistance, or not at all. Observed clusters contain 33.7% of selected members in cluster-critical regions, compared with 21.6% in TNG-Cluster, while their Major-to-Minor ratios are similar. Outside these regions, observations contain substantially more Intrinsic and Boosted Lenses and fewer Inert Members, with Boosted Lens fractions of 25.8% and 13.5%, respectively. The discrepancy persists at fixed subhalo mass and after including line-of-sight structure. A mass-conserving contraction mimicking core-collapsed self-interacting dark matter largely recovers the conditional lensing fractions but not cluster-critical occupancy. The GGSL discrepancy therefore reflects both insufficient central concentration in simulated members and differences in their locations within the cluster lensing field.

2610.14987.abstract: We present a detailed chemo-dynamical analysis of the chemically peculiar very metal-poor ([Fe/H]$=-2.22\pm 0.11$) Milky Way (MW) halo star, 2MASS J00101758$-$1735387 (hereafter J0010-1735), discovered by the $R$-Process Alliance. We derive abundances for 45 elements, including 28 neutron-capture elements, and confirm that \thestar\ is highly $r$-process-enhanced, with [Eu/Fe]=$+1.30$. The light, $\alpha$, and Fe-peak element abundances ratios relative to Fe are all sub-solar, aside from C, Si, and most extremely, Ca. We investigate three possible formation scenarios based on the star's chemical abundances and orbital kinematics: whether it formed in the \textit{in-situ} MW halo, in a MW dwarf galaxy satellite, or in a satellite of the Magellanic Cloud system. Using the position of \thestar\ in the [Mg/Mn]--[Al/Fe] plane, the abundance pattern of both the light and heavy elements, and the kinematics, we conclude that J0010-1735 most plausibly originated in a now-disrupted ultra-faint dwarf galaxy that was accreted into the MW halo. We examine potential chemical enrichment scenarios of J0010-1735, including one similar to the $r$-process-enhanced UFD Reticulum II, or enrichment via a sub-Chandrasekhar Type Ia SNe, potentially supplemented by a Ca-rich gap transient and by a separate neutron-rich site that facilitated $r$-process enrichment. A nuclear cosmochronometric age of $12.5\pm4.2$ Gyr is derived from the [Th/Eu] ratio, consistent with an ancient origin in one of the earliest star-forming systems in the universe.

2610.15939.abstract: Asteroseismology of $\delta$ Sct stars has strong potential for determining the ages of young stars through individual mode fitting. We present a neural-network emulator trained on approximately 46 million rotating pulsation models. From stellar mass, metallicity, age, and equatorial rotation velocity, it predicts 12 classical observables, two asteroseismic scalars, and the p mode, f mode and low-order g mode frequencies for degrees $\ell=0$-3, including the individual $m$ components of rotationally split multiplets. We couple the emulator to nested sampling through a multivariate likelihood that propagates correlated emulator residuals, making full Bayesian posterior exploration practical. Applied to five $\delta$ Sct stars in the Pleiades observed by TESS, the framework gives mutually consistent individual asteroseismic ages of 107-117 Myr. Combining their age posteriors gives a cluster age of $113.3\pm4.5$ Myr (statistical), consistent with the $112 \pm 5$ Myr lithium-depletion-boundary age and the 110-160 Myr range from rotating-isochrone fitting. Together with spectroscopic $v\sin i$, the inferred equatorial velocities also provide post-fit inclination estimates. Separate perturbed-grid tests using 100 matched synthetic pairs per input-physics variation give median absolute age shifts of $2.1$, $2.3$, and $5.2$ Myr for $|\Delta f_{\rm ov}|=0.005$, $|\Delta\alpha_{\rm MLT}|=0.1$, and $|\Delta Y|=0.02$, respectively; the corresponding 90th percentile shifts are $6.5$, $7.6$, and $16.2$ Myr. These tests describe conditional population sensitivities, not a systematic uncertainty on the Pleiades age. Together, the cluster-age agreement and the scale of these input-physics sensitivities support $\delta$ Sct asteroseismology as a complementary age estimation method for young stars.

2610.16527.abstract: Broad-lined H-rich superluminous supernovae (SLSNe II) tend to show signs of interaction, including a UV excess compared to a blackbody function. However, a quantitative analysis of the CSM configuration and the UV excess has so far not been performed for most of the literature sample. Additionally, SN 2023gpw showed signs of asymmetry in its peculiar blackbody and spectral evolution, raising the question of whether similar properties can be found in other SLSNe II. We aim to characterize the circumstellar environment of SLSNe II by searching for signs of asymmetry, quantifying the UV excess, and investigating any IR echoes produced by dust. Diversity among SLSNe II is also explored. We fit blackbody functions to the SEDs of SLSNe II to quantify the UV excess luminosity and its evolution. We use this to investigate mass-loss rates required to produce the excess through interaction. We also investigate the line profiles in SLSN II at late times and compare line velocities to the blackbody radius evolution. We examine public WISE IR images and place constraints on IR echoes. We find mass loss rates of $\sim10^{-4}$ to $\sim0.03\, \mathrm{M_\odot}$~yr$^{-1}$ when assuming all interaction luminosity emerges in the UV, i.e., conservative lower limits for the total mass loss rate. Radii calculated from line velocities in late-time spectra are mostly too large for a spherical interaction photosphere, only compatible with the blackbody radius evolution if the CSM is non-spherical with a low filling factor. This is in some cases supported by a mismatch between spectroscopic and blackbody expansion velocities. Considerable diversity is seen in the sample, probably as a result of different viewing angles and CSM masses. WISE images seem too shallow to observe IR echoes in SLSNe II beyond $z\sim0.1$, but in the nearest event, SN 2020jhm, a likely IR echo is detected, suggesting pre-existing dust.

2610.17013.abstract:
Indirect searches for dark matter (DM) span gamma rays, charged cosmic rays, neutrinos, X-rays, radio emission, the cosmic microwave background (CMB), and the 21~cm signal, but reported constraints and anomalies vary in evidential strength. This critical review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature from January 2000 through October 2026 using a structured search strategy.
We assess observations through a framework linking particle interactions and halo source terms to propagation or cosmological energy deposition, instrumental response, background modeling, and statistical inference. Fermi-LAT observations of dwarf spheroidal galaxies provide robust GeV-scale benchmarks for DM annihilation, whereas Galactic-center searches offer higher expected signals but depend more on foregrounds and halo profiles. Charged-cosmic-ray measurements are precise but limited by propagation and source uncertainties, while neutrino searches offer complementary sensitivity through solar capture, directional and flavor information, and high-mass annihilation or decay. Several widely discussed signals, including the 3.5~keV line, 511~keV emission, the Galactic-center GeV excess, charged-particle features, cluster radio excesses, and candidate gamma-ray lines remain inconclusive because of limited independent confirmation, uncertain target scaling, spectral degeneracies, or background-modeling limitations.
Cosmological observations provide complementary constraints from CMB energy-injection limits and 21~cm measurements of the intergalactic medium. Artificial intelligence increasingly supports reconstruction and inference but requires rigorous calibration and domain-shift validation. The strongest case for DM discovery would require statistically consistent evidence across independent targets, instruments, or messengers, under common particle-physics parameters, and with well-characterized uncertainties.

2610.17022.abstract: The Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will observe our Universe on the largest scales and so enable the study of fundamental assumptions in cosmology, such as cosmic homogeneity and isotropy. Observations over recent years have reaffirmed an unexpected challenge to the Cosmological Principle first seen in measurements of the cosmic radio dipole. This dipole anisotropy is thought to be caused by our local observer motion, however, it is observed to be about three times larger than predicted, with significances exceeding 5$\sigma$. The SKA is in a unique position to shed light on this anomaly by measuring this and other effects related to our observer motion. To quantify this, we forecast the capability of large-angle HI and continuum surveys of the SKA to constrain the kinematic matter dipole in galaxy number counts, the modulation of the matter power spectrum by a kinematic dipole, and kinematic spectral distortions of diffuse radio emission.

2610.17081.abstract: The Transition Matrix formalism (T-matrix) offers an optimal solution to the problem of radiation scattering and absorption by particles characterized by a high degree of chemical and structural complexity. However, its application to particle models composed by large numbers of constituents has been classically limited by the substantial computational burden of the method. As a consequence, the investigation of light scattering and absorption processes, in cases where particle asymmetry and non-homogeneity play an important role, typically need to rely on simplifying assumptions which affect the correct interpretation of transmission spectra and extinction curves. This problem has a huge impact on many fields of scientific application. In particular, it has a critical role in astrophysics, because the ability to model highly non homogeneous particles is a fundamental requirement to understand the role of extinction in different phases of the interstellar medium (ISM), as well as to probe the physics of light transmission in planetary atmospheres within the Solar System and beyond. In this work we describe the application of a new implementation of the T-matrix formalism, based on the framework originally developed by Borghese, Denti & Saija and named Nano-particle Transition Matrix code, which leverages the power of modern hardware architectures to reduce the computational costs related to the solution of relevant particle models for the investigation of dust in the ISM and of hot-Jupyter class planets atmospheric aerosols. This new implementation of the T-matrix formalism can handle calculations of increasing complexity with a direct impact in the interpretation of the transmission spectra of transiting exoplanets produced by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and of those expected from the Atmospheric Remote-sensing Infrared Exoplanet Large survey (ARIEL).

those of the models. Vertical line in each panel marks the 0 km s-1 velocity.

2610.17140.abstract: The Type II SN 2024ggi is one of the nearest core-collapse SNe to have exploded in recent decades. Its proximity has enabled extensive multiwavelength monitoring from early times through the nebular phase. Signatures of late-time interaction between the SN ejecta and hydrogen-rich circumstellar material (CSM) have recently been reported. Here we extend its study using late-time optical photometry and spectroscopy from 570 to 820 d after explosion. We investigate the emergence and evolution of late-time ejecta-CSM interaction and constrain the geometry of the interaction region and the properties of newly formed dust. Comparisons with other interacting SNe II and with synthetic spectra are presented. We model the H$\alpha$ profile with the Monte Carlo radiative-transfer code Damocles, including both gas and dust components. Spectroscopic signatures of interaction precede the photometric flattening. The spectra evolve from ejecta-dominated to interaction-dominated as H$\alpha$ develops a broad, boxy profile. The optical light curves subsequently flatten relative to the $^{56}$Co decay rate at approximately 650-670 d. The emission lines show a systematic blue-to-red asymmetry that requires a dust component newly formed within the ejecta. The inferred dust mass formed in the ejecta is $10^{-6}-10^{-5}$ M$_\odot$ if the grains are amorphous carbon or a carbon-silicate mixture, but can reach up to $10^{-3}$ M$_\odot$ for pure silicates.

2610.17200.title: Interpreting the stacked kinetic SZ signal II: the degeneracy between satellite galaxies and baryonic feedback

figures.caption: Figure 1: Halo occupation distributions of the three DESI-like mock samples: LRGs (blue), BGS (orange), and ELGs (green). The stellar-mass-selected samples (LRGs and BGS) exhibit pronounced high-halo-mass tails, whereas the ELG sample has a broader halo mass distribution. The high-mass end of each distribution is dominated by satellite galaxies.

Figure 2: Decomposition of the mean optical depth around satellite galaxies of our DESI LRG-like sample (Table 2). The total signal (black) is decomposed into contributions from the isotropic (radial, orange) and anisotropic (azimuthal, purple) satellite distributions within the host halo. The top panel shows the optical depth profiles, while the middle and bottom panels show the ratio of each contribution to the total optical depth around satellites. The isotropic component arises from the spherically averaged gas within the host halo evaluated at the radial position of satellites, and dominates the total signal (bottom panel). This strongly depends on the radial distribution of satellites within the host halo (dashed lines): assuming that all satellites are located at the halo centre (virial radius) overestimates (underestimates) the signal by $\approx 40\%$ ($\approx 60\%$) at the virial radius. The anisotropic component (solid purple) is primarily sourced by the anisotropic gas distribution around the host halo traced by the satellite positions, while the contribution from gas bound to the satellite subhalos (dotted purple) is subdominant.

Figure 3: Impact of baryonic feedback on the mean optical depth around central (left panel) and satellite galaxies on our DESI LRG-like sample (Table 2). The latter is decomposed into isotropic (spherically averaged gas profile of the host halo evaluated at the radial position of satellites within the host, middle panel), and anisotropic (extra contribution from the anisotropic distribution of gas around the host halo traced by satellites, right panel) constributions.
The upper panels show the mean optical depth, and the lower panels show the percentage difference relative to the case in which gas traces the dark matter (black curves). Coloured curves correspond to models with different baryonic feedback strengths, and the vertical dashed lines mark the mean virial radius of the corresponding halo population. Baryonic feedback redistributes gas from halo centres to larger radii, suppressing the optical depth on small scales and producing more extended profiles (left and middle). Around satellites, this suppression is shifted to larger projected radii due to the radial distribution of satellites within their host haloes (middle). The anisotropy of gas is smaller than that of dark matter, in a largely baryon feedback independent way and dominated by hydrodynamical processes such as pressure (right).

Figure 4: Contribution of stacks around central (orange) and satellite (green) galaxies to the total optical depth (blue) around DESI-like LRG (left), BGS (middle), and ELG (right) samples. Upper panels show the mean optical depth profiles, while lower panels show the fractional contribution of the central and satellite components to the total signal. The horizontal dashed line marks equal ($50\%$) contributions, and the vertical dashed line the effective virial radius of each sample. Although the satellite fraction in all three samples is considerably smaller than $50\%$, they contribute at least half of the total optical depth (for LRGs and ELGs), and dominate the signal in the BGS sample, accounting for up to $\approx 80\%$ of the signal across all scales.

Figure 5: Impact of baryonic feedback and satellite galaxies on the stacked optical depth profiles around DESI LRG, BGS and ELG-like samples. Solid coloured curves show the profiles for varying feedback strengths, stacked on central-only samples. The dotted points show the profile in a fiducial feedback scenario ($f_{\rm gas}$), stacked in galaxy samples including satellites. The associated error bars correspond to the statistical uncertainty of DESI DR2 $\times$ ACT measurements (Qu and others, 2026; Hadzhiyska and others, 2026). The upper panels show the profiles, and the lower panels the ratio to the fiducial feedback scenario stacked on centrals only. Baryonic feedback and including satellites in the stacking sample impacts the optical depth profiles to a comparable amplitude.

Figure 6: Inferred halo gas fractions obtained by fitting kSZ profiles stacked on centrals and satellites with a model calibrated on centrals only. The gas fractions of the mock data are shown in green, and the inferred ones in black shaded area and dashed line. Thin blue lines show the halo gas fractions of the other FLAMINGO feedback variations for reference. Each column corresponds to a DESI-like sample, with the vertical line indicating its mean halo mass. Ignoring satellites in the modelling biases the inferred gas fractions low, with the largest bias for BGS, followed by LRGs, while no significant bias is found for ELGs due to the large errorbars of the measurements.

Figure 7: Comparison of theoretical and statistical errors on the stacked kSZ profiles, for DESI LRG-like (left), DESI BGS-like (middle) and DESI ELG-like (right) samples at three angular distances from the galaxy positions. The theoretical errors are computed from a) fully agnostic model about the satellite distribution within the host haloes (orange), and b) the error done by neglecting the contribution from anisotropic gas traced by satellites (purple). The statistical errors come from DESI DR2 $\times$ ACT measurements (Qu and others, 2026; Hadzhiyska and others, 2026) (grey). The dominant theoretical error arises from the unknown radial distribution of satellites within the host, dominating over the statistical uncertainty on small scales for LRG and BGS-like samples. The anisotropic contribution is comparable or subdominant to the current statistical uncertainties ($1-1.5\sigma$ effect), but expected to become significant with upcoming measurements.

Figure 8: Sensitivity of the stacked kSZ profiles to uncertainties in the satellite fraction for DESI LRG, BGS and ELG-like samples. We assess the impact of uncertainties on the satellite fraction by randomly removing increasing fractions of satellite galaxies while simultaneously removing low-mass central galaxies to keep the mean halo mass of the sample fixed. For each perturbed sample, we measure the deviation of the stacked kSZ profile from the profile obtained using the fiducial satellite fraction. We quantify this deviation as a function of the fractional error in the satellite fraction using the covariance matrix of DESI DR2 $\times$ ACT measurements (Qu and others, 2026; Hadzhiyska and others, 2026). For the LRG and BGS samples, fractional uncertainties of $\approx 10\%$ in the satellite fraction already produce deviations of $\approx 1.5\sigma$ and $\approx 3\sigma$, respectively, from the fiducial profiles.

Figure 9: Accuracy of the emulator assessed with a leave-one-out test. Each feedback variation is removed from the training set in turn, and the emulator is rebuilt from the remaining variations. We plot the predicted kSZ profile for the held-out variation, given its halo gas fraction, divided by the true kSZ profile. Curves show the largest fractional error across feedback variations at each angular scale, for each DESI-like sample (colours). Solid lines correspond to interpolation, where the held-out run is bracketed by the remaining training set. Dashed lines correspond to the two ends of the feedback ladder, $f_{\rm gas}+2\sigma$ and $f_{\rm gas}-8\sigma$, which are extrapolations when held out. The interpolation is accurate at the $1-2\%$ level, while the extrapolation is below the $6\%$ in all angular scales.

Figure 10: End-to-end test of the emulator. The fiducial feedback variation is held out from the training set, and its kSZ profile is fitted to infer the halo gas fractions. We show the ratio of the posterior halo gas fractions to the real halo gas fractions. Colours correspond to the DESI LRG-like, BGS-like, and ELG-like samples, and the vertical dotted line is the mean halo mass of each. In all samples, the true halo gas fractions are recovered within the $1\sigma$ posterior.

2610.17200.abstract: The kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) signal stacked around a galaxy sample traces the gas around halos and is a powerful probe of baryonic feedback. Its interpretation, however, depends on the satellite galaxies in the sample. Using the FLAMINGO hydrodynamical simulations and DESI-like samples of luminous red galaxies (LRGs), bright galaxies survey (BGS), and emission-line galaxies (ELGs), we show that satellites and feedback have similar effects: both suppress the small-scale signal. This degeneracy arises because stacking on satellites, which are offset from the centre of their host haloes, mimics the extended gas distribution produced by feedback. Although satellites make up only 20-30% of each sample, they account for 50-80% of the signal because they occupy more massive halos than centrals; thus their imprint on the stacked profiles can be as large as that of feedback. At the precision of current DESI$\times$ACT data, neglecting satellites in the modelling biases the inferred gas fractions low, by up to a factor of two, and overestimates the feedback strength, particularly for the LRG and BGS samples. Remaining agnostic about the satellite population avoids this bias but reduces the constraining power, so robust constraints would require knowing the satellite fraction to better than 10%, for instance from lensing and clustering data of the same galaxy samples. Finally, a further contribution from satellites will become statistically significant with upcoming surveys: satellites trace the anisotropic gas distribution around their host haloes, an effect that contributes 10% of the signal, and will likely require simulation-based models to capture.

2610.17212.title: MRI Turbulence versus $α$-Viscosity in Circumbinary Disks: Implications for Gravitational-Wave Dephasing and Accretion Variability

2610.17212.abstract: Our understanding of gas torques on massive black hole binaries (MBHBs) relies on hydrodynamical (HD) simulations of circumbinary disks (CBDs) in which an $\alpha$-viscosity models angular momentum transport. However, CBDs around MBHBs near merger are hot, magnetized plasmas where transport is driven by magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) turbulence sustained by the magnetorotational instability (MRI). We test how well an $\alpha$-viscosity captures MRI turbulence with 3D global Athena++ simulations of a locally isothermal CBD around an equal-mass, circular MBHB, run in HD and MHD from the same initial torus on identical grids, so that only the transport mechanism differs. Excising the region within twice the binary separation, $r<2~a_{\rm bin}$, allows $1000$ orbits of evolution, several times longer than previous MHD simulations. Both disks deliver the same accretion rate, and the gas beyond $2~a_{\rm bin}$ exerts a positive torque in both, yet the MHD torque is $3.5$ times larger and $3$ times more variable. Near the midplane, transport is similar in the disk body but three times weaker in MHD at the cavity edge, where $2$-$3$ times more mass piles up in a more eccentric cavity, raising the torque. The accretion rate is modulated mainly at twice the binary frequency in HD, but by a persistent lump at the cavity edge and its beat with the binary in MHD. The outer-disk torque therefore implies a contribution to the gas-induced phase shift in the gravitational-wave signal of LISA binaries $3.5$ times larger than in $\alpha$-disk models, and a different variability signature for LSST and Roman.

2610.17218.abstract: Population III (Pop III) stars link the chemical enrichment of the early Universe to the formation of the first massive black holes, yet their evolution remains poorly understood at extreme masses. Using GENEC, we evolve rotating zero metallicity models from $500$ to $1000\,M_\odot$ at $v/v_{\rm crit}=0.1$ through core Si burning, and a $1000\,M_\odot$, $v/v_{\rm crit}=0.4$ model evolved through He exhaustion. In the fiducial $1000\,M_\odot$ model, convection and rotational transport carry freshly synthesized C and O into H burning layers, producing $62.1\,M_\odot$ of primary N by He exhaustion. Surface mass loss removes $20.2\,M_\odot$, including $1.8\times10^{-3}\,M_\odot$ of N, with $\log(\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{O})=0.68$, $\log(\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{C})=1.48$, and $\log(\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{O})=-0.80$. By the final hydrostatic model, the inner $100\,M_\odot$ is confined within $0.088\,R_\odot$ while the photosphere remains several thousand solar radii away. As C, Ne, O, and Si burning accelerate, chemical mixing freezes out and advanced products remain buried beneath the envelope. At core Si exhaustion, the central angular velocity reaches $4\times10^{-3}\,{\rm s^{-1}}$ while the surface rotates at $5.25\times10^{-8}\,{\rm s^{-1}}$, a contrast of $7.6\times10^4$. Contraction drives this spin up, while inner specific angular momentum changes by less than $1\%$. The maximum $j_{\rm eq}/j_{\rm ISCO}$ is $0.313$, limiting disk formation in our inside out estimate. These models show that Pop~III stars can produce strong primary N signatures and rapidly rotating black hole progenitors while their envelopes determine which products enrich the early Universe.

2610.17248.title: Scaling Up: A Global Optical/X-ray Correlation For Reprocessing Across Black Hole Masses

The solid line represents the best-fit relation (Eq. 5).

(b) The inclination-corrected correlation ($L_{V}$ vs. $a_{R}\cos i\ L_{X}^{0.5}$).

2610.17248.abstract: This study extends the optical/X-ray correlation from black hole low-mass X-ray binaries (XRBs) to active galactic nuclei (AGN), bridging scales from stellar-mass to supermassive black holes (SMBHs). In XRBs, optical emission predominantly originates from the thermal reprocessing of high-energy photons on the surface of the geometrically thin, optically thick accretion disk. The reprocessed optical luminosity follows a power-law relation of the form $L_{V} \propto L_{X}^{\beta} a$, with $\beta \sim 0.5$, where $L_X$ is the X-ray luminosity and the orbital separation $a$ serves as a proxy for the disk size. To test the universality of this relationship across all mass scales, we analyzed quasi-simultaneous X-ray and optical flux data from a sample of XRBs and AGN that have estimates of the radius of the optically emitting disk. To bridge the structural differences between these populations, we utilized the characteristic optical/X-ray time lag derived from reverberation mapping as a physical proxy for the reprocessing radius. Our analysis reveals a tight, global correlation across all black hole masses, described by $\log L_V = 0.48\log L_X + 0.96\log a_R + 6.5$ with a scatter of $\sim 0.20$ dex, where $a_R$ is the reprocessing radius derived from the lag. Incorporating a geometric correction for the disk inclination angle ($\cos i$) slightly reduces this scatter to $0.18$ dex. These results suggest that X-ray reprocessing is scale-invariant across accretion disks, from stellar-mass black holes to SMBHs. This scaling relation provides new constraints for models of X-ray emission regions in accreting black holes.

Figure 3: Dependence of the inferred upper limit on $f_{\mathrm{BH}}$ on the assumed value of $\epsilon$; the fraction of RV-variable non-BH systems that evade our follow-up tests and classification. For the fiducial model, we adopted $\epsilon{\simeq}0.235$ as a conservative lower estimate.

Figure 4: Distribution of inferred stellar masses in the OB parent sample. The sample is limited to massive stars with inferred $M_{\mathrm{OB}}{\geq}10\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$. 2610.17253.abstract: Binaries composed of a luminous OB star and a black hole (BH) are a key evolutionary link between massive stellar binaries and merging compact-object binaries, but only a handful are known and their occurrence fraction remains poorly constrained. We use multi-epoch spectroscopy from the SDSS-V Milky Way Mapper to place a first rigorous empirical upper limit on the fraction of Galactic massive ($\geq 10\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$) OB stars with a close BH companion, $f_\mathrm{BH}$. Radial-velocity (RV) variability alone cannot distinguish BH companions from the far more numerous luminous binaries. We therefore combine the SDSS-V RV variability measurements of 3130 massive OB stars with high-resolution follow-up and literature information to identify luminous companions among the RV-variable subset. Forward-modelling the detectability of OB+BH systems using BH masses and orbital parameters from binary-evolution models, we find $f_\mathrm{BH} \lesssim 3\%$ at 95% credibility. This empirical upper limit approaches, but does not exclude, theoretical predictions for the OB+BH fraction. The constraint is primarily limited by the number of RV-variable systems that can be decisively classified, highlighting the importance of complete, high-quality follow-up for future searches.

2610.17415.abstract: The Leavitt & Pickering (1912) mean period-magnitude relation for SMC Cepheids exhibits correlated residuals relative to modern Gaia $B_G$ and Johnson $V$ photometry ($r_{\delta V/\delta L12}\approx0.76$). Therefore dispersion inherent to Leavitt's photographic photometry relation is not solely random scatter ($\sigma_{L12,B_G,V}=0.22\pm0.03,0.25\pm0.04,0.20\pm0^{m}.03$), and is potentially consistent with the partial encoding of combined effects from the elongated SMC, classical Cepheid instability strip, differential reddening, etc. OGLE data indicate that $\gtrsim870$ SMC variables identified by Leavitt (1908, Table 2) are classical Cepheids ($\gtrsim 90$ %), and the preliminary unphased Table 2 photometry likewise features correlated residuals relative to contemporary observations ($r_{\delta B_G/\delta L08-T2}\approx0.54$). Table 6 data in Leavitt (1908, $n=16$) define a highly linear Leavitt law over an extensive baseline ($r\approx-0.98$), but constitute a smaller sample than the later 1912 work ($n=25$).

2610.17741.abstract: We present the first targeted Einstein Probe (EP) X-ray observations of any planetary nebula (PN). Using the onboard Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT), we detect X-ray emission within the central region of IC 1297. The spectral analysis yields a plasma temperature of $kT = 0.086^{+0.054}_{-0.058}$ keV ($T\sim1.0 \times 10^{6}$ K), characteristic of shocked wind bubbles in PNe, whereas there is no evidence that its Wolf-Rayet central star emits X-rays. The absorption-corrected X-ray luminosity in the 0.3--2.0 keV energy band is $L_{\mathrm{X}} = 2.8 \times 10^{32}$ erg s$^{-1}$, also consistent with a hot bubble. At an adopted distance of $\sim3.8$ kpc, IC 1297 is the most distant X-ray emitting PN found to date, opening up a new observational window on hot-bubble formation and evolution. It is also among the most luminous known X-ray-emitting PNe. Our results demonstrate the capability of the EP FXT for detecting and characterizing faint, extended X-ray sources in the soft X-ray band for distant PNe, extending the known spectral properties of detectable X-ray emitting PNe. We also compiled the X-ray properties of all 41 known Galactic XPNe, finding a clear correlation between distance and X-ray luminosity that reflects an observational bias toward detecting the brightest sources at large distances. The compilation also shows a separation in X-ray luminosity between hot bubbles powered by H-rich and [WR]-type central stars, with the latter reaching luminosities up to an order of magnitude higher. The ten most luminous XPNe all host [WR]/PG 1159 central stars.

2610.18146.title: Low-frequency spectra and scattering of pulsars towards the Gum Nebula with the MWA

Red plus symbols mark the six pulsars analysed in this work. The black circle indicates the approximate optical boundary of the Gum Nebula (Chanot and Sivan, 1983; Woermann et al., 2001, e.g.), the cyan circle marks the Vela supernova remnant, and the orange circle shows the approximate extent of the IRAS Vela Shell (Sahu, 1992; Woermann et al., 2001, e.g.). The background image is based on the composite H$\alpha$ map of Finkbeiner (2003), which combines the Virginia Tech Spectral-Line Survey (Dennison et al., 1998), the Southern H-Alpha Sky Survey Atlas (Gaustad et al., 2001), and the Wisconsin H-Alpha Mapper survey (Haffner et al., 2003) at an angular resolution of $6\arcmin$.

Figure 2: Representative pulse profiles of the six pulsars detected in ObsID 1331293096, shown in consecutive 2.56 MHz sub-bands. The profiles have been baseline-subtracted, normalised to unit peak amplitude, and vertically offset for clarity, so the plotted amplitudes represent relative rather than absolute intensity. The pulse phase is shown over one full rotation cycle. Several sources show stronger asymmetric broadening towards lower frequencies, consistent with increasing interstellar scattering.

Figure 3: Broadband radio spectra of the six pulsars. Blue circles show the MWA measurements; literature measurements use the symbols identified in each panel. Grey dashed, black solid, and magenta solid curves show the best-fitting PL, FFA, and turnover-constrained BPL models, respectively; shaded regions are the 16th–84th percentile Monte Carlo bands. Residuals are in units of the propagated log-flux uncertainty used in the primary fits. The three MWA points at $u\leq 132.48$ MHz for PSR J0742$-$2822 and the 108.16 MHz point for PSR J0835$-$4510 are plotted as excluded measurements: their pulse broadening makes recovery of the period-averaged intrinsic flux density unreliable.

In the left-hand panels, black and orange curves show the observed profiles and best-fitting forward-convolution models, respectively; dashed curves show residuals and orange shading shows the 68% model bands. For PSR J0820$-$4114, both intrinsic components and all seven sub-bands were fitted simultaneously; the annotated $\tau_{\rm sc}$ values are correlated values implied by the global scattering law. In the right-hand panels, solid lines show the fitted free-index scattering laws and dotted lines show the reference $\tau_{\rm sc}\proptou^{-4}$ scaling. For PSR J0820$-$4114, black points are the band-wise free-$\tau_{i}$ diagnostics, while the orange curve and bootstrap bands come directly from the global joint profile fit; all seven sub-bands, including 240.00 MHz, are retained. The sensitivity of the fitted index to frequency selection and to fitting only the second, trailing component is reported in Appendix Table 7.

Figure 5: Joint scattering analysis of PSR J0835$-$4510 (the Vela pulsar). Panel (a): Model comparison for the tested combinations of convolution scheme, pulse-broadening function, and number of intrinsic Gaussian components, expressed as $\Delta$AIC and $\Delta$BIC relative to the optimum under each criterion. Panel (b): Profile stack and adopted fiducial model. Panels (c) and (d): Bootstrap distributions of the scattering index $\alpha_{\rm sc}$ and normalisation $\tau_{{\rm sc},0}$. The one-component thick-screen solution with circular convolution minimises the BIC and is adopted as the fiducial model; the corresponding two-component solution minimises the AIC.

Figure 6: Summary of the spectral turnover analysis. (a) Peak frequencies of the conditional FFA solutions; the comparison source PSR J0630$-$2834 is not assigned a Gum-related FFA peak. Error bars show the 16th–84th percentile Monte Carlo intervals. (b) Diagnostic EM intervals obtained from the FFA fits for $T_{\rm e}=3\times 10^{3}$–$10^{4}$ K. Filled symbols denote Gum-direction pulsars and the open symbol denotes J0630$-$2834. Blue and orange bands show the smooth-shell estimates from Purcell et al. (2015) with and without the filling factor, respectively; dashed lines mark their central values. (c) Improvement of the preferred turnover model over the PL, $\Delta{\rm AICc}_{\rm PL-turnover}={\rm AICc}_{\rm PL}-\min({\rm AICc}_{\rm FFA},{\rm AICc}_{\rm BPL})$; the open bar again marks the comparison source. All quantities use the propagated measurement uncertainties, and the fit for the Vela pulsar excludes 108.16 MHz.

Figure 7: Comparison of the scattering indices measured in this work with representative literature values. The dashed horizontal line marks the reference scaling $\alpha_{\rm sc}=-4$, commonly associated with a simple thin-screen approximation. The measurements for PSR J0742$-$2822 are broadly consistent with earlier low-frequency studies in showing a flatter-than-canonical scattering spectrum. The PSR J0820$-$4114 value is the effective index from the joint two-component thin-screen analysis. For the Vela pulsar, the value shown here is an effective index inferred within the preferred joint thick-screen modelling framework and should therefore not be interpreted in exactly the same way as the single-source thin-screen measurements for the other pulsars.

Figure 8: Comparison of the public YMW16 v1.3.2 and NE2025/mwprop v2.0.4 electron-density models along the Gum Nebula pulsar sight lines. Filled circles and open squares represent the NE2025 and YMW16 predictions, respectively. (a) Ratio between the model DM distance and the independent distance estimate. The error bars propagate the asymmetric uncertainties of the independent distances; uncertainties in the model predictions are not included. (b) Ratio between the model-predicted and observed scattering timescales at 150 MHz. The model values are taken from the DM-to-distance evaluation at the observed DM and are scaled from 1 GHz using a common $u^{-4}$ dependence to compare the model normalisations. PSR J0820$-$4114 is omitted from panel (a) because it lacks an independent distance, and PSR J0630$-$2834 from panel (b) because it lacks a directly comparable broadening measurement. The Vela pulsar (PSR J0835$-$4510) is excluded from the scattering comparison because its measured broadening is obtained from a thick-screen model and is not directly comparable with the thin-screen measurements. Dashed lines indicate equality between the model predictions and observations.

Figure 9: Comparison between measured scattering timescales and empirical $\tau_{\rm sc}$–DM relations for the six-pulsar sample. Panel (a) shows the empirical predictions from Bhat et al. (2004) and Cordes et al. (2022), scaled from 1 GHz to 150 MHz, together with observed values where a directly comparable thin-screen measurement is available. Panel (b) shows the predicted-to-observed ratios for those four pulsars; the dashed horizontal line marks equality. PSR J0835$-$4510 is excluded from the ratio panel because its broadening was derived from a joint thick-screen fit and is not directly comparable to the thin-screen measurements.

2610.18146.abstract: Context. The Gum Nebula is a nearby ionised complex with sight-line-dependent pulsar propagation. Aims. We test whether a smooth ionised structure can explain low-frequency spectral turnovers and pulse broadening, or whether smaller-scale material is required. Methods. We analysed Murchison Widefield Array observations of six pulsars at 80--240 MHz, combining sub-band flux densities with literature data. We compared power-law, free--free absorption (FFA), and turnover-constrained broken-power-law (BPL) spectra, and modelled scattering through pulse-profile convolution. PSR J0820-4114 and the Vela pulsar were fitted jointly across frequency. Results. All six spectra depart from a single power law. FFA is favoured for PSRs J0737-3039A and J0820-4114, and BPL for J0742-2822 and J0835-4510; the other two classifications depend on assumed error floors. Conditional FFA solutions imply emission measures of $10^4$--$10^5$ pc cm$^{-6}$ for electron temperatures of $3\times10^3$--$10^4$ K, far exceeding smooth-shell expectations. PSRs J0737-3039A and J0837-4135 have scattering laws consistent with $\tau_{\rm sc}\proptou^{-4}$. We obtain $\alpha_{\rm sc}=-3.07\pm0.11$ for J0742-2822 and $-1.59\pm0.44$ for J0820-4114 using a joint two-component model. The Vela pulsar is best described by an effective thick-screen model with $\alpha_{\rm sc}\simeq-2.74$. Neither tested Galactic electron-density model reproduces both independent distances and low-frequency scattering uniformly. Conclusions. The results favour a structured Gum--Vela magneto-ionic environment in which neighbouring sight lines probe different absorbing and scattering material; these effects need not arise in the same plasma component.

2610.18278.abstract: State-to-state rate coefficients for inelastic molecular collisions are essential inputs for non-local thermodynamic equilibrium radiative transfer models, yet their computation using quantum scattering methods is prohibitive for large molecules and highly excited rotational states. We investigate the ability of artificial neural networks to extend existing datasets of collisional excitation rate coefficients without performing additional scattering calculations. A multilayer perceptron model was trained using molecular quantum numbers, level energies, energy gaps, and kinetic temperature as descriptors, and optimized on logarithmic rate coefficients. The model was tested on diverse collision systems ranging from simple diatomic molecules (CO, SiO) to open-shell species (SO), small asymmetric tops (H$_2$O, SO$_2$), and complex organic molecules (benzonitrile and vinyl cyanide) colliding with H$_2$ molecules or He atoms. Extrapolations were performed toward higher rotational levels, higher temperatures, and combinations of both. For most systems, predictions of rate coefficients involving previously unseen rotational states yielded mean error factors between 1.1 and 1.5, with the dominant rate coefficients generally reproduced more accurately than weaker transitions. Temperature extrapolations proved particularly successful, while combined extrapolations in temperature and rotational levels remained accurate to within a factor of two in most cases. The prediction quality depends on the interplay between dataset size, temperature range, molecular complexity, and the presence of clear collisional propensity rules. Overall, the approach demonstrates that machine learning can provide a practical route to extending collisional datasets for astrophysical applications, especially for large molecules for which additional quantum-scattering calculations are computationally demanding.
